title: Bodies of unseen beings and the world of suspended images (vol. II, pp. 54–56)
en:
**Jinn and devils according to the corporeal account.** Jinn are described as subtle airy bodies able to assume different configurations and produce remarkable effects. They include believers and unbelievers, obedient and disobedient beings. Devils are said to be fiery bodies which induce corruption by reminding people of the attractions of sin and sensual pleasure and causing them to forget the benefits of obedience. The Qurʾānic statement attributed to Satan—that he possessed no compelling authority but called people and they responded, so they should reproach themselves—is used to clarify the limits of such influence. Another account makes angels, jinn and devils all bodily composites of the four elements, though fire predominates in devils and air in the others. Elemental composition need not always approach a balanced temperament. One of the four elements may dominate in differing degrees, so that the composite tends toward the realm of earth, water, air or fire and ordinarily remains there unless moved by choice or by some further cause. Because air and fire are so subtle and translucent, these bodies are imagined as entering narrow openings and even the interior of a human being without being visible. They become apparent to ordinary sight only when clothed in thicker earthy or watery coverings, presenting themselves in human or animal shapes.

Angels are said to help people accomplish what would otherwise exceed bodily capacity, such as overcoming adversaries, flying through the air or walking over water, and to preserve the vulnerable from dangers. Jinn and devils are said to associate with certain human beings in practices of sorcery, talismanry, enchantment and the like. **Objections** to the corporeal theory are evident. If such beings are elemental composites, why are they not ordinarily visible to healthy eyes, like other compounds? If their bodies are so fine as to be invisible, how could they ever appear, or avoid being dissolved by slight disturbances? Persistent and repeated reports of their appearance to prophets and saints, of conversation with them and of their surviving for a long time in storms or narrow spaces are appealed to by the proponents. Moreover a determinate bodily species and temperament ordinarily produce determinate bodily forms; how can one individual assume many different shapes?

The answer rejects the alleged necessary consequences. On the theology of a freely choosing creator, God may cause certain observers to see them under some conditions but not others and preserve or change their bodies by His power. Even a philosopher who treats natural processes as necessitated might suppose a mixture sufficiently dense to be visible to some eyes but not others, a temporary thicker bodily covering, a special soul or substantial form preserving their constitution and varying their shape under different conditions, or an intelligence capable of avoiding destructive conditions such as winds. Merely explaining subtlety as *transparency without tenuity* fails to accommodate traditions of passing through small openings and appearing in strikingly different sizes. These are possible reconciliations of reported experiences with a corporeal hypothesis, not an independent demonstration that the hypothesis is true.

**Conclusion: the world of suspended images (*ʿālam al-muthul*).** Certain metaphysically inclined philosophers, attributing their doctrine to ancient sages, posit an intermediate world between the sensible and intelligible worlds. It is neither separated in exactly the manner of wholly immaterial intellects nor immersed in matter like sensible bodies. In it every existent—including separate substances, material bodies, accidents, movements, rest, positions, forms, tastes and smells—has a self-subsisting **suspended exemplar**, an image having determinate appearance without inhering in physical matter or an ordinary subject. It becomes visible through a **manifesting locus**, such as a mirror, imagination, water or air; it may appear through different loci and cease to appear when a mirror breaks, the image fades or the observer's directed attention is lost. The world is described as vast or without end, with its own imaginal celestial motions and elemental and composite forms receiving effects from the motions of its exemplary heavens and illuminations from the intellective realm.

Ancient accounts of an extended world of magnitudes other than the sensible world, containing innumerable wonders and immense cities named **Jābalqā and Jābarsā**, are adduced. Angels, jinn, devils and uncanny beings are sometimes explained as exemplary forms themselves or as separate rational souls manifested through them. Through this intermediate world, immaterial realities allegedly appear in many shapes, beautiful or ugly, luminous or dark, according to the capacities of what manifests them and of what perceives them. The same theorists explain bodily resurrection through an **imaginal body** directed by the separated soul, possessing sensory faculties and undergoing bodily pleasures and pains; luminous suspended forms manifest the bliss of the righteous and dark ones the suffering of the wretched. Dream images, waking imaginations, delirious visions, and experiences in great fear are also interpreted as appearances from this realm rather than as ordinary external bodies. Extraordinary reports concerning saints being seen in distant places, appearing from closed rooms or apparently transporting people and objects instantaneously are treated as further alleged manifestations of this intermediary order.

The proponents appeal either to mystical disclosure and experience or to an argument about reflected and imagined images: such images appear not to be sheer nothing, nor material things in the mirror, nor pure separate intelligibles (because they have apparent magnitude), nor images impressed literally in a tiny brain (because a huge object appears in a small place). Hence, they conclude, the images must belong to a distinct world. The commentator rejects the demonstration: the proposed conclusion is very ambitious, but the supporting reasoning is weak, especially given the already stated objections to the impossibility of a small representation displaying something much larger. Leading philosophers and theologians have therefore not accepted the argument as decisive.

**End of Division IV — the following source begins the fifth division, on Divine Matters (*al-ilāhiyyāt*).**

title: First chapter, Investigation 1: establishing the Necessary Existent
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. II, pp. 56–58; canonical source characters 1038666–1043261 (exclusive).

The fifth objective concerns divine matters: investigations relating to the very essence of God Most High, what is to be denied of Him, His attributes, what may and may not be affirmed of Him, His acts, and His names. The author therefore arranges it in six chapters. The first establishes the proofs for the existence of the Necessary Existent and investigates whether His essence is different from all other essences.

**The philosophers' route to the Necessary Existent.** It is beyond doubt that something exists. If this is necessary in itself, the sought conclusion follows. If it is possible in itself, there must be a cause by which its existence is preponderant. The same question is raised about that cause. Either a circle or an infinite regress follows—both impossible—or the series reaches a necessary existent, as required.

**The theologians' route.** The world has been shown to be originated. Indeed, an originated thing exists; every originated thing necessarily requires one who brings it into existence. Its originator either depends upon another, leading to a circle or infinite regress, or the chain reaches something eternal, with no need for a cause whatsoever: this is what is meant by the Necessary Existent.

Both arguments rest upon the impossibility of a possible or temporally originated thing occurring without an originative cause, and upon the rejection of causal circularity and regress. Since the theologians do not admit an eternally existing contingent thing, establishing an eternal originator establishes a necessary existent. One cannot simply oppose them with the philosophers' permitted infinite succession of temporally arising celestial motions and configurations. First, that succession has already been considered in the debate over the world's origination; second, the proposed infinite succession concerns **effects**, not a hierarchy of independently producing **causes**, whose relevant existence must coincide with the existence of their effects.

Some have supposed that the Necessary Existent could be demonstrated **without** rejecting a possible occurrence's becoming actual without a determining ground (*tarajjuḥ bilā murajjiḥ*). They argue that there must be among existents something which does not depend on another—lest circularity or regress ensue—and that this is precisely what 'necessary' means. But this is disputable: independence of *another* does not by itself entail intrinsic impossibility of nonexistence unless groundless alternation has been excluded. Otherwise an independently existing thing might exist at one time and fail to exist at another, neither state proceeding from its own essence or from something else, but arising by sheer happenstance.

Others have supposed that a proof is possible **without** independently rejecting regress. Several arguments are presented and examined.

**First argument.** If there were no necessary existent, everything existing would be possible. Possible things would then have to exist through their own essences, which is impossible. **Assessment.** That consequence follows only if possible things are not each dependent upon another possible thing without end; otherwise the very issue is the rejected infinite regress. If the argument concerns the *totality* of possibles considered together, it still must show that the totality's cause cannot be itself or one of its parts but must lie outside it. That too introduces an argument against regress rather than eliminating the need for one.

**Second argument—the totality of possibles.** Take together all possible things so that not one falls outside the totality. The totality is possible, according to the preceding argument. Every possible thing necessarily has an **independently sufficient producer**, one possessing all conditions of efficacious production. Such a producer cannot be the totality itself, obviously. Nor can each component be independently productive of the whole, for that would allow several complete causes for one effect, and would make a thing cause itself and the causes on which it depends: the independent producer of a composite must produce every constituent, since any constituent produced by a different independent cause would defeat the asserted sufficiency. Nor can *one* component serve as that sufficient producer. First, it would have to cause itself and its own causes; second, it is itself dependent on another component by hypothesis, and therefore not independently sufficient; third, if one component were sufficient, its own cause would seem prior and still more fit for the same role, with no basis to designate the component alone. The producer must therefore lie **outside** the totality of possibles, and what lies outside all possible things is necessary. **Assessment.** This is in fact the first of the previously discussed arguments against infinite regress, with its qualifications and replies; restating it does not dispense with that argument.

**Third argument—the necessitating cause of the totality.** The aggregate of possibles is possible, and every possible thing requires a cause through which its existence becomes necessary: a possible thing does not exist until its existence is necessitated, as explained earlier. The necessitating cause of a totality composed solely of possibles cannot be a component of it, since each component depends upon a cause of its own and so is not independently necessary merely by being present. The necessitating cause must be outside the totality, hence necessary in itself. This differs from an aggregate including the Necessary Existent: in the latter there is a component which can be specified as the source of necessitation. The formulation can also be restated negatively: the totality requires an independent cause whose presence excludes its nonexistence, and none of its parts has this character. **Assessment.** Again, the argument returns to a proof against regress. It can be challenged by the claim that, in an infinite ordered succession, the existence of every downstream effect is necessitated by what precedes it, without one separate exterior cause being identified by the proposed reasoning.

**Fourth argument—the complete cause of an originated event.** The complete cause of a new effect must be present at the instant of the effect's origination, because an effect cannot fail to follow its complete cause, nor precede it. If that complete cause were entirely contingent and did not include the Necessary Existent, either it would have a cause outside itself, in which case it would not be *complete* relative to the effect, which likewise requires that additional cause; or it would have no such cause. In the second case, if the cause could not previously exist, its later appearance would seem to turn intrinsic impossibility into possibility; if it could previously exist, its restriction to the particular time would appear to be a determination without a determining cause. **Assessment.** The dilemma is defective in two ways. First, one must determine carefully whether the temporal qualification attaches to the cause's existence or to its impossibility and possibility; the alleged transition and groundless determination do not follow without further argument. This parallels earlier objections concerning whether an originated thing's absence from pre-eternity entails intrinsic impossibility. Second, the same temporal puzzle arises even if the complete cause **includes** the Necessary Existent, or is the Necessary Existent considered with respect to this effect. Thus the proposed argument does not distinguish the cases it is meant to distinguish.

**Translation note.** The movement from existence to necessary existence is a reported argumentative structure, not a declaration that al-Taftāzānī finds every formulation successful. His repeated *fīhi naẓar* ('there is a difficulty with it') is retained as a criticism rather than flattened into approval.

title: Investigation 2: signs of the Maker and persuasive proofs
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. II, pp. 58–59; canonical source characters 1043261–1046550 (exclusive).

The existence of the Maker has already been established by demonstrative arguments. Here the author adds arguments of the **persuasive** kind and observes that belief in a Maker is among the generally acknowledged convictions which scarcely anyone of recognized standing has opposed. This multiplication of considerations is appropriate because the existence of the Maker is among the most important and exalted objects of inquiry.

No one doubts the existence of the world of bodies: celestial spheres, stars, the elements, and their mineral, vegetable, and animal compounds, with the variations of their qualities and states. From the **possibility** or **origination** of these things, and from the possibility or origination of their qualities, one may argue for an eternal, powerful, wise Maker. These yield four familiar paths of consideration. The Qurʾān directs attention to them in many places: the creation of the heavens and earth, alternation of night and day, ships moving across the sea, the life-giving rain, varieties of living things, the winds and clouds, the sun, moon, stars, diversity of languages and colours, the genesis of human life, and signs on the horizons and in human beings themselves. The indications encompass the higher world with its supposed celestial configurations and motions, the lower world with the dispositions and mixtures of elements, atmospheric and terrestrial phenomena, mineral and vegetable life, animals, and especially the human body described in anatomy and the human soul described in psychology.

What underlies these routes is that the dependence of a **possible** thing upon a producer and an **originated** thing upon an originator is self-evident to natural understanding, and that what produces extraordinary, intricate and well-ordered effects is attributed to a powerful and wise agent.

**Objection.** Even allowing all this, why may the Maker not be a spiritual substance belonging among contingent beings, rather than the transcendent Necessary Existent? There are several replies.

**First.** The mind may apprehend by intuitive estimate that the producer of such things must be absolutely rich or self-sufficient, everything depending upon Him while He depends on nothing; His existence would then be through His own essence. This remains a **persuasive** route, but the accumulation of many mutually supporting persuasive indications may strengthen probability to the point of certainty.

**Second.** Rational consideration leads one from an observed maker to that maker's own originator. If the maker is the Necessary Creator, the aim is reached; if itself created, its creator has still greater title to power and wisdom. This cannot proceed without end once the arguments against infinite regress are brought to bear. Hence the succession terminates in the Necessary Existent. The Qurʾān's recurrent description of the signs as addressed to those who **understand** is appropriate here.

**Third.** The purpose of these scriptural invitations is to alert those who do not acknowledge a Maker who is the origin of all things and their ultimate end, who commands and forbids, and to whom all have recourse when hope in created beings fails. Scripture also points to the human tendency to call sincerely upon God amid danger, and to the admission that God is the creator of heaven and earth. The purpose is to show that the conclusion is supported by decisive and persuasive reasons and is also widely acknowledged—sometimes by natural disposition, sometimes through elementary arguments. The famous illustration says that dung indicates a camel and footprints indicate a traveller; how could the star-filled heaven and the earth's paths fail to indicate the Subtle, All-Aware Maker?

The source then reports a view ascribed to certain *malāḥida* who do not deny a cause of the world in the ordinary sense; rather, they place the alleged supreme source beyond **every pair of opposites**, such as existence and nonexistence, unity and multiplicity, necessity and possibility. In the name of transcendence, they decline to call that source even 'existent', 'one', or 'necessary'. Al-Taftāzānī rejects this as evidently false. The attribution should remain cautious: the text supplies a polemical description, not a secure independent identification of a named school in this passage.

title: Investigation 3: the Necessary Existent is unlike possible essences
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. II, p. 59; canonical source characters 1046550–1047738 (exclusive).

The correct position is that the Necessary Existent Most High differs from possible things **in essence and reality**. For if the Necessary and the contingent were alike in reality but distinguished by a particular feature, necessity and possibility would either be concomitants of the common essence, in which case both would have to share the same status, or belong to the essence together with its distinguishing feature, in which case the Necessary would be composite, contrary to necessity through itself.

His essence nevertheless agrees with the essences of possible things in that the **concept** of 'essence'—here, what subsists through itself and in which other attributes may subsist—is correctly predicated of them all, as an **accidental predicate** of its subject, not as a common constituent of their specific realities. Similarly the existence of the Necessary and the existence of the possible, despite their difference in reality according to the account being discussed, share the *general concept* of existence, predicated of both as an extrinsic concomitant rather than a constitutive part.

The customary arguments for a shared concept of existence—the possibility of dividing existence into necessary and possible, certainty concerning existence as such while hesitating over the particular kind, and the unity of the contradictory opposite—show no more than that the **concept of essence or existence can be shared**. They do not prove that the realities so conceived are essentially alike.

Some theologians, by contrast, maintain that the divine essence resembles other essences and is distinguished by four *states* (*aḥwāl*): necessary existence (sometimes named necessity), life, complete knowledge, and perfect power; or by a fifth state called *divinity* which gives rise to the four. title: Investigation 4: divine beginninglessness and endlessness
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. II, pp. 59–60; canonical source characters 1047738–1048329 (exclusive).

The claim that the Maker is **beginningless and endless** may be treated as a separate question in this chapter. Once a Maker necessary through Himself has been established, however, there is no further need for an independent proof: the necessity of existence entails the impossibility of nonexistence, whether from eternity or at any future time.

Certain theologians establish only that the world has a Maker, without first deciding whether that Maker is necessary or contingent. They must therefore separately establish His beginninglessness and endlessness. For the first, they say that if He were originated He would need an originator, leading to regress; they also undertake to show that God is the immediate producer of the world's existence, without intermediary. For the second, they argue that what is beginningless cannot cease because it is either necessary in itself or terminates in what is necessary through a process of necessitation, whereas what proceeds through free choice would, on the premise being invoked, be preceded by nonexistence. The complexities of that last premise have been examined previously and are not resolved simply by its repetition here.

title: Chapter 2, Investigation 1: divine unity and the negation of composition
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. II, pp. 60–64; canonical source characters 1048329–1058565 (exclusive).

The second chapter concerns **transcendence** (*tanzīh*): the denial of everything unbefitting the Necessary Existent. Its first investigation denies multiplicity in God, whether **composition from parts**, as though He were compounded of two or more, or **numerical plurality**, as though there existed two or more necessary beings.

### Against composition

Everything composite depends upon its constituents, and each constituent is other than the composite. Whatever depends upon another is possible in itself, since its essence taken without that other is not sufficient for its existence—even if that other is not an external efficient producer. Moreover, each constituent would either be necessary, giving several necessary beings, which will be refuted, or contingent, rendering the alleged Necessary dependent upon a contingent thing and thus even more clearly contingent. Again, either one constituent requires the other, in which case the composition involves dependency incompatible with necessity, or neither requires the other, in which case they fail to constitute one reality, just as a stone placed beside a person does not thereby make a single substance.

### Arguments against several necessary beings

**First.** If necessity belonged to two, they would have to be distinct, since there cannot be two without distinction. What distinguishes them must be other than what they share. Each would therefore be composed of what is common and what is distinctive: impossible of the intrinsically Necessary. **Objection.** This would follow only if the common necessity were an essential constituent; could it not be an accidental concomitant, shared by two beings otherwise distinguished? **Reply.** The Necessary's necessary existence is identical with its quiddity under the account employed here. If necessity were an accident inhering in its essence, that accident would be contingent and caused by the essence, unless caused by something else, in which case necessity would not be intrinsic. If caused by the essence, the explanation would require priority to itself in existence and necessity. Necessity is thus the very quiddity; shared necessity would mean shared quiddity, and shared quiddity with distinguishable individuality would make a composite.

If one says that the individuating difference is merely an accident, ask what gives rise to it. If it follows from the common essence or from attributes belonging to that essence, the supposed two necessary beings cannot be different in the proposed way. If it follows from an independent external cause, dependence upon that other defeats intrinsic necessity. This latter reasoning may be treated as an **independent second proof**: if the individuating determination is identical with, caused by, or inseparably implied by the necessary essence, there can be no distinct second necessary being; if it requires an external cause, the bearer is not necessary in itself.

**Third.** If there were two necessary beings, each would have its own determination or individual identity (*taʿayyun, huwiyya*). Necessity and determination must either imply one another, or they do not. If no implication holds, there could be necessity without individual determination—which is impossible for an existent—or determination without necessity, incompatible with necessity's being intrinsic. If there is implication, and necessity is caused by determination, the priority of cause would make necessity prior to itself; if determination is additional, intrinsic necessity would derive from another. If determination follows from necessity, or both are grounded in the essence, each determination would be inseparable from the one necessary essence and the proposed plurality vanishes. If both derive from an external cause, necessity is no longer intrinsic. The stages of the dilemma require the same caution about conceptual and real priority developed in earlier divisions.

### Arguments from divine agency

**Fourth.** Here begins a series of theologians' proofs. Suppose two gods possessed the attributes of divinity—knowledge, power, will, and the like—and both proceeded to produce the same determinate object, such as the motion of a given body at a given time. Either the effect occurs through both, leading to the unacceptable concurrence of two **independently sufficient agents** upon one effect; or through only one, in which case there is an ungrounded preference between agents equally disposed to the possible effect. It will not suffice to say that this effect never occurs, because that would display their incapacity; nor to say that it occurs through their combined powers, *neither* being independently sufficient, since the hypothesis attributes complete divine power and will to each.

**Fifth—the proof of mutual hindrance (*burhān al-tamānuʿ*).** Suppose one god wills the motion of a body. Can the other will its opposite, or not? If yes, suppose he actually does. Either both wills attain their objects, producing contradictory or contrary states together; or neither attains its object, showing both supposedly omnipotent agents unable to act—and, in an appropriate example such as motion versus rest at one moment, leaving the substrate without one of the alternatives; or only one attains its object, leaving the other incapable and assigning victory without a determining ground. If the other cannot even will the contrary, then he lacks power over something possible in itself, and therefore is not divine.

**Objection.** Opposition to the other's will may become impossible under the particular conditions, just as a body already occupying one place cannot simultaneously occupy a second. How does the lack of power to do what has become impossible imply incapacity? **Reply.** A possible thing does not turn into an intrinsically impossible thing. What is impossible in the spatial example is the **combination** of opposed locations at once, not either location considered alone. Likewise here the combination of the opposed divine wills is impossible, not each will separately. The contradiction consequently arises from positing two deities with equal unbounded powers.

**Further objection.** Both would know every good and evil consequence. If the interest or benefit lies on one side, both must will it, not opposing outcomes. **Reply.** Even granting that will always follows the best interest, consider a case where the two opposing possibilities are equal in merit. **Further objection.** Even with only one divine agent, when an effect has already been produced, He cannot produce again *that very existent effect*, for producing what is already existent is impossible. Would this not annul His divinity? **Reply.** Not producing an effect a second time because His power has already achieved it is an indication of perfected power, not incapacity. Being prevented from realizing one's will by another agent is a genuine frustration of power.

This is called the proof of mutual hindrance. Al-Taftāzānī relates it to Qurʾān 21:22, concerning the corruption which would follow if heaven and earth had gods beside God. If *corruption* means the **failure of heaven and earth to come into existence**, the argument is that with multiple divine agents the world's production could be assigned neither to both combined nor to each independently nor to one alone. If corruption instead means the **dissolution of the existing order**, the argument appeals to the normal expectation of conflict, rivalry and divergent works from rival powers. The harmonious coordination of parts through which the world forms one ordered whole would be lost. The latter form invokes an order-of-nature consideration, not exactly the same demonstrative structure as the first.

**Sixth.** If the two agreed in producing every effect, there would be an unacceptable overlap of independently sufficient agency; if they disagreed, the contradictions of mutual hindrance would follow: incapacity in both, or incapacity in one together with unjustified preference. **Seventh.** If two deities existed, whatever differentiates them could not be a concomitant of divinity common to both. It would have to be separable, so plurality might disappear and the two become one, which is impossible. **Eighth.** One is sufficient and there is no evidence for a second; the proposed second is therefore to be denied, lest innumerable groundless possibilities be admitted—such as saying that everyone observed today is a distinct individual from the person observed yesterday. Objections to this epistemic argument include that the absence of evidence is not universally evidence of absence. Several replies are reported, including restricting the argument to what has no possible evidence, but al-Taftāzānī considers this approach weak.

**Ninth.** If plurality were admitted, no one number would have a greater claim than any other, and the number of gods would be unbounded. This is supposed to contradict prior demonstrations of the finitude of all existing multitudes. The argument's weakness has also been noted previously. **Tenth.** Prophetic mission and the establishment of prophetic truth through miracles do not presuppose that divine unity has *already been known*. Scriptural proof may therefore be drawn from the concordant call of the prophets to worship one God and from the decisive revealed texts against partnership. To insist that no prophet can be known without first knowing that the Necessary Existent is one confuses the **fact** that necessity entails unity with the **epistemic necessity** of first recognizing unity before proving the prophetic mission. The distinction is between a truth's obtaining and somebody's knowledge that it obtains.

### Conclusion: the scope of *tawḥīd*

The reality of *tawḥīd* is believing that God has **no partner in divinity or in the proper prerogatives of divinity**. Muslims do not dispute that the governance of the world, the creation of bodies, deserving worship, and the beginninglessness of a self-subsistent entity belong among those prerogatives. 'Beginninglessness' here means not being preceded by nonexistence; if it means not being preceded by another cause, it comes to the same thing as intrinsic necessity or divinity.

The theologians of the author's school maintain beginningless **attributes** without positing separately existing divine substances beside God; moreover, they do not simply identify each attribute with the essence in the unqualified way their opponents allege. The Muʿtazila attribute to creatures the production of their own acts, not the creation of every other accident or body. Al-Taftāzānī nonetheless regards the attribution to Satan of substantial control over evils against the divine will—even if Satan's power is created and permitted—as a grave difficulty. More problematic still, from his point of view, is the philosophers' doctrine that separate intellects are eternal and productive of souls or bodies, with governance of the elemental world delegated to intellects and celestial spheres. On that account, unity seems reduced to the assertion of **one intrinsically Necessary Existent**, without the same exclusive account of divine creation as that defended by Sunni kalām. The Muʿtazila emphasize the denial of a plurality of beginningless entities; the Sunni theologians the denial of a plurality of creators. All agree, at least in the sense defined here, in denying a plurality of necessary beings, of beings worthy of worship, and of independent creators of bodies.

Among the views rejected are forms of **dualism** positing light as the source of good and darkness as the source of evil; other accounts speak of Yazdān and Ahriman, disputing whether Ahriman is eternal or produced by Yazdān. Their objection is that one source of good and evil would itself be both good and evil. The reply distinguishes being *predominantly good or bad* from being the **producer of acts or events described as good or bad**: the latter does not entail the former. An opposing dilemma asks whether the good principle is unable to remove evil, or can do so and chooses not to. If the dualist says the existence of evil has a hidden wise purpose, the same possibility may be urged concerning God's permitting events called evil or bad. These are the text's dialectical arguments, not a full independent historical account of every religious community here mentioned.

Regarding worship of angels, stars, and idols, the text reports possible explanations: supposed delegated celestial powers, representations of tutelary spirits or heavenly bodies, talismans fashioned at rare auspicious moments, images embodying imagined divine or angelic corporeality, or commemorative images of revered deceased persons later approached for intercession. The account also treats Christian and Jewish attributions of divine sonship polemically. If the transmitted language of 'father' and 'son' is authentic and free of alteration, al-Taftāzānī reads it figuratively as lordship, origin and return, complete direction toward God, or the conferral of special honour, not biological derivation or partnership in the Godhead. He closes by affirming that divine partnership is excluded by reason and revelation, and exclusive entitlement to worship by revelation.

**Editorial qualification.** The text's labels for other communities and theological opponents reproduce its medieval polemical framing. They must not be mistaken for neutral, independently verified descriptions of those communities' doctrines. The opening proof of the intrinsic necessity of divine unity and the subsequent proof of conflict between agents differ in their premises; the translation retains that distinction. The printed-source and clause-level audit remains pending.

title: Chapter 2, Investigation 2: God is not a body, accident, or spatial substance
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. II, pp. 64–67; canonical source characters 1058565–1066283 (exclusive).

The Necessary Existent is **not a body**. Every body is composite: either of intelligible parts (genus and difference), of real principles (matter and form, or indivisible substances), or of quantitative portions. Every composite depends upon parts, and nothing dependent upon another is necessary through itself. Neither is He an **accident**, since an accident requires a subject which sustains it: in this technical discourse that is precisely what it means for something to be an accident. Nor is He to be called a **substance** in the particular categorical sense. For a substance is explained either as a spatially situated thing needing no recipient, or as a quiddity which, if it exists, exists *not in a subject*. On the latter definition, existence is additional to its quiddity, whereas the Necessary Existent is not thus constituted, as established earlier.

He is neither **in a place** nor **in a direction**. According to one account a place is the inner boundary of the encompassing body touching the outer boundary of what it encompasses; according to another it is the vacant spatial extension occupied by body. A direction is the terminus toward which pointing or motion is directed. These notions apply to bodies and corporeal things, not to the Necessary Existent.

Some theologians, particularly the older authorities, employed a different route for these negations. The technical name *substance* was explained as that from which something is constituted, and *accident* as what cannot endure. In the sensible world it may be true that every self-subsistent thing is a substance and every other-dependent thing an accident; but, they argue, the **names** do not owe their application simply to those abstractions. They appeal to usages in which *jawhar* means original stock or noble nature, and *ʿāriḍ* means a passing or impermanent occurrence. Hence they do not call the divine eternal attributes 'accidents' despite their dependence upon the divine essence in the relevant sense.

### Further proofs against corporeality

The theologians add four arguments. **(1)** Every body is temporally originated, as argued already. **(2)** Every body is spatially situated, whereas the Necessary is not. **(3)** If the Necessary were a body He would either possess all corporeal qualifications, including mutually contrary ones such as motion and rest; possess none, in which case some necessary corporeal qualifications would be missing; or possess some rather than others, requiring an external determiner or an ungrounded preference. **(4)** Every body is finite, as demonstrated in the discussion of extension, and thus bounded by a particular **shape**, the manner in which its boundary encompasses it. It cannot have all shapes, and its possession of one without another would again require an extrinsic ground or yield groundless specification. **Objection.** Does the same reasoning invalidate God's possession of His attributes rather than their opposites? **Reply.** The divine attributes are perfections belonging to Him by virtue of His essence, while their opposites are deficiencies excluded by that same essence. The possible contrary states of bodies may have equal title to occurrence and thus require determination.

### Further proofs against place and direction

**(1)** If God occupied a region, the region would have to be beginningless: nothing occupying a region can exist without one. But all things other than God and His attributes have been shown to be originated. **(2)** If He were in a place, He would depend upon it and become contingent. The place, however, can be thought of as independent of its occupant, for an empty place is conceivable. It would then be independent of the alleged Necessary and still more independent of what depends upon Him, producing an unacceptable rival necessity. Both these arguments presuppose that region or place is a **real existent**, not merely a supposed extension. **(3)** If the Necessary occupied a location or direction, He would either occupy all regions and directions, introducing impossible superposition and unsuitable contact with impure things, or some rather than others, again requiring an extrinsic determiner or a groundless preference.

### Names, anthropomorphism, and the equivocation of spatial imagination

To call God a *body* simply with the intention of saying that He **exists** violates ordinary and technical Arabic usage. Yet *substance* in the broad meaning 'that which exists through itself' or simply 'essence' is an attested philosophical convention, which explains occasional philosophical language of divine substance and certain expressions attributed to Ibn Karrām. Even so, one should not venture to call God either a body or a substance in these misleading senses: revelation has not authorised such speech, and the terms invite the erroneous ideas of the corporealists or the doctrine of one substance in three hypostases ascribed to Christianity in the text.

Those who genuinely affirm that God is a body or is in a place and direction rely, according to al-Taftāzānī, upon **false judgements of imagination** (*qaḍāyā wahmiyya kādhiba*) and upon scriptural expressions apparently suggesting location. title: Chapter 2, Investigation 3: union, indwelling, and the meaning of annihilation (*fanāʾ*)
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. II, pp. 67–69; canonical source characters 1066283–1071690 (exclusive).

The Necessary Existent cannot **be united with** another thing, nor can He **inhere** in it. Union (*ittiḥād*) is excluded by the previously established impossibility that two genuinely distinct existents become numerically one: it would make the Necessary identical with the possible and the possible identical with the Necessary, an evident contradiction. Several grounds also exclude *indwelling* (*ḥulūl*).

**First**, what inheres in another is in some respect dependent on its recipient, whether the example be a body occupying a place, an accident subsisting in a substance, a form inhering in matter on the philosophers' account, or an attribute belonging to a qualified substance. Dependence on another contradicts the Necessary's intrinsic necessity. **Objection.** Sometimes *indwelling* may mean intermixture, like rosewater in the rose. **Reply.** This belongs to physical bodies and entails spatial composition and division; in the relevant respect it returns to body occupying place.

**Second**, if His indwelling in a subject were necessary, He would depend on that subject, so the subject too would be beginningless—and, on the reasoning offered, even necessary. If the indwelling were only contingent, then what is intrinsically independent of the subject could become dependent upon it, allegedly reversing the very relation of independence. Al-Rāzī's reported proof is open to objections. In the first case God could, it is argued, cause the subject and His own relation to it by virtue of His essence, without dependence on His effects; a producer's necessary effects do not make the producer dependent upon them. In the second, one need not assume that every kind of being *in* something entails dependence upon that particular subject; a given body can be in a particular region without being intrinsically dependent upon **that** region.

The proof can be recast: what is intrinsically independent of any subject cannot inhere in it, since an inhering item depends upon its recipient; if the Necessary were not intrinsically independent, He would be contingent. **Objection.** Lack of intrinsic independence does not itself entail *intrinsic* dependence, since both dependence and independence might be relational states arising with other conditions. **Reply.** The mere lack of intrinsic independence suffices for contingency, because what is necessary through itself is necessarily independent through itself. The argument does not require the additional premise that dependence is intrinsic. Another reconstruction asserts that if the supposed indwelling being were intrinsically dependent it would be contingent, and otherwise its indwelling impossible. The response is that not being intrinsically dependent need not exclude acquiring a dependent relation under some conditions.

**Third**, if indwelling is not a perfection, it must be denied of God; if it is a perfection, then God would be **perfected by another**, which all parties reject. **Fourth**, indwelling in another, in the sense commonly admitted, is a kind of spatial or subject-dependent presence; extending it to God threatens to make Him spatially situated. Divine attributes do not refute this: philosophers deny their distinct reality in the relevant sense, and theologians refuse to call divine attributes accidents *inhering in* the divine essence. They say they **subsist through Him** (*qāʾima bi-dhātih*) in a manner of qualifying dependence (*ikhtiṣāṣ nāʿit*).

**Fifth**, were He to inhere in a body, either He would pervade all its parts, making Him divisible, or be present in one part, making Him smaller than other bodies or parts. Both alternatives are rejected. **Sixth**, on the atomistic theory in which bodies share the same fundamental atomic nature, the hypothesis would permit divine indwelling in the smallest or most abject bodies; it would remove any secure basis for rejecting indwelling in a mosquito or the like.

The impossibility applies to the **divine essence** and still more to divine **attributes**, since an attribute cannot depart from its essence. The author enumerates the possible mistaken combinations: indwelling of the divine essence or a divine attribute in a human body or spirit, and union of the essence or attribute with that body or spirit. He next describes doctrines attributed to Christians and to certain groups identifying themselves with Islam. These accounts are explicitly **polemical classifications made by the medieval author**, and not a historically sufficient account of the beliefs of every Christian or of modern Islamic schools.

His report of Christianity describes a single substance and three hypostases—existence, knowledge and life—identified in the account with Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He then reports various interpretations of the Incarnation as mixing, illumination, substantial transformation, manifestation, conjunction of divinity and humanity, or alternating union and separation. He rejects the doctrines in the form in which he has described them. His reports about certain extreme Shīʿī views and some alleged Sufi doctrines likewise criticize the literal manifestation of God in a human being, or the literal union of a person with God, and claims that such union abrogates obligation and prohibition.

### Two positions which merely *seem* to involve union

There are, however, **two further doctrines** whose language may suggest union or indwelling although they do not, in their own intended formulations, assert literal physical or substantial blending.

The **first** concerns the traveller who has reached the culmination of the journey *to* and *in* God. Such a person may be immersed in the sea of divine unity and knowledge, until awareness of his own self and attributes seems to disappear before awareness of God and His attributes. He becomes absent from consideration of anything other than God and sees nothing in existence except God. This is called **annihilation in unity** (*al-fanāʾ fī al-tawḥīd*). The celebrated divine saying concerning the servant's drawing near through supererogatory acts until God loves him, and becomes his hearing and sight, is invoked to indicate this condition. Someone undergoing it may use words suggesting union or indwelling because ordinary language is inadequate to disclose the condition. Al-Taftāzānī does not simply condemn this phenomenon: he writes with humility that he stands upon the shore of wishing, drawing from the sea of unity what he can, and acknowledges that the path to this annihilation is **direct witnessing (*ʿiyān*) rather than discursive proof (*burhān*)**. He closes, 'God is the giver of success.'

The **second** asserts that the Necessary is **absolute existence** (*al-wujūd al-muṭlaq*) with no plurality in it, and that multiplicity exists only in relations and determinations, like appearances of imagination or a mirage. The whole is one reality recurring in manifestations without physical admixture and appearing multiple to observers without real division. In this scheme there is no literal *union* or *indwelling*, because in its own ontology there are not two distinct realities to be united or to have one in the other. Al-Taftāzānī nevertheless regards the extended discussion of this doctrine as departing from the method of reason and revelation; he refers back to his earlier criticism in the discussion of existence. This is **not** the same evaluation he has just expressed of experiential *fanāʾ*. The distinction between a state of mystical experience and a metaphysical claim that the Absolute alone is real must be preserved.

**Translation note.** In the source the objections to the second proof are attributed to the 'Imām' and to subsequent critics. Their dialectical force does not make them the final adopted doctrine. Terms such as *ḥulūl*, *ittiḥād*, *fanāʾ*, and *wujūd muṭlaq* have not been conflated. The passage has been translated from the electronic source; full printed-edition collation and verification of the reported group-attributions are pending.

title: Chapter 2, Investigation 4: can the Necessary be the locus of originated attributes?
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. II, pp. 69–71; canonical source characters 1071690–1076477 (exclusive).

The majority deny that the Necessary Existent can be qualified by an **originated entity** (*ḥādith*)—one which exists after previously not existing—contrary to the position here ascribed to the Karrāmiyya. But this denial does **not** exclude every changing truth predicated of God. New **negations** and **relations** may be affirmed: He is not the provider of one person who has died and is provider of another who has been born. Likewise, one may speak of real attributes with **changing objects of relation**: He knows this newly originated thing, can act upon it, and so forth. On the doctrine of Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī, one may also speak of relational *states* which obtain when new objects of knowledge appear. These distinctions will be clarified later.

Such qualifications answer al-Rāzī's allegation that **all schools** are in effect committed to God's being a locus of originated things. The Ashʿarites speak of God's becoming the producer of Zayd and of new predications about His knowledge, vision and audition once Zayd and his acts exist. The Muʿtazilites speak of novel relations of willing, disliking, hearing, and seeing; certain doctrines add new states of knowing as objects of knowledge arise. The philosophers speak of God as prior to, simultaneous with, and posterior to new events as those events appear and perish. Yet **not every relation is a distinct extra-mental existent**. A newly true description does not automatically insert a newly created positive quality into the divine essence. That is the exact point in dispute, and the examples are not decisive without further ontological argument.

One argument for permitting such an originated attribute says: whatever makes it possible for a **property** to subsist in the Necessary must be either the general character of being a property, in which case it applies alike to eternal and originated properties, or that character together with eternity, which is merely a negative notion—the absence of a beginning—and so cannot contribute to causal efficacy. The reply rejects the dilemma: the particular quiddity of an eternal attribute may itself differ from that of an originated attribute, even though the two share the generic intelligible notion of being a property. Furthermore, eternity could be a **condition** of admissibility, or origination an **impediment**, without either being a producing positive ingredient.

### Arguments denying originated attributes

**First—the argument from perfection.** If it were possible for God to acquire an originated attribute, He could suffer a deficiency. If the newly acquired attribute were a perfection, then being without it while able to possess it would have been a defect; but He lacked it before it arose. If it were not a perfection, His possessing it would be incompatible with the agreed principle that all real divine attributes must be perfections. **Objection.** Being without *this* perfection need not be defective if God always possesses another perfection of the same kind, and the ending of one instance is the necessary condition of another's beginning. A continuous sequence of individual perfections without beginning or end—like the philosophers' model of celestial movements—would leave no interval of privation. **Reply.** The original premise is asserted to be near self-evident. Moreover, if every individual perfection is originated, it does not follow that its type is an actual beginningless perfection. To say God has no beginningless instance but is always characterized by such new instances puts an originated state perpetually in the subject, while each originated individual is absent at the putative pre-eternal limit. These responses themselves depend upon the positions previously taken concerning beginningless succession.

**Second—the philosophers' principal argument.** Acquiring an originated quality involves **change**, and change cannot be predicated of God. **Objection.** If *change* means merely passing from one description to another, the major premise merely repeats what is disputed. If it means change in the divine essence's necessary character, or receptively undergoing alteration through another thing, the minor premise is denied: the originated predicate might be produced by the divine essence itself, either voluntarily or through a necessitating order in which one successive perfection becomes possible upon the disappearance of its predecessor. The third chapter concerns **positive or affirmative attributes** (*al-ṣifāt al-wujūdiyya*). The Necessary Existent's being described by *negative* notions—for example, being one, separate from body, and not in a region or direction—does not of itself establish any additional real attribute. Neither do relational names and names derived from divine acts, such as the Exalted, the Great, the First, the Last, the One who withholds and grants, lowers and raises. The controversy instead concerns **real affirmative attributes**, such as His knowing and His power.

According to the people of truth, God possesses **eternal attributes additional to the essence**. He is knowing by knowledge, powerful by power, living by life, and likewise hearing, seeing, and speaking, with some disagreement about the precise status of individual attributes and their relations to one another. They avoid, however, the assertion of a plurality of **independently beginningless beings**. Even among those who agree that the attributes are not simply identical with the essence, there is hesitation over saying without qualification that they are *other* than it, or other than one another. Some decline to call the attributes 'beginningless' (*qadīma*) although they are eternal (*azaliyya*), preferring to say that God is beginningless **with His attributes**. They prefer 'subsisting through His essence' (*qāʾima bi-dhātih*) or 'existent through His essence' to 'in Him', 'with Him', 'adjacent to Him', or 'inhering in Him', all of which could suggest spatial separation or an independent second entity. The attributes are not called **accidents**.

Most philosophers and Muʿtazilites oppose this addition of attributes. Some describe God as living, knowing and powerful **through His essence**, others by a unique state (*ḥāl*) belonging to Him, or without assigning any additional causally explanatory attribute. Al-Taftāzānī notes the extraordinary subtlety and possible ambiguity of al-Rāzī's own treatment. In the *Maṭālib al-ʿĀliya*, al-Rāzī says that the principal problem is defining the exact disagreement. One school posits three things in knowledge: **subject, knowledge, and knowledge's relation to its object**. Another inserts the status 'being knowing' (*ʿālimiyya*) in addition to knowledge, perhaps with one or two relations, producing four or five distinguishable considerations. Al-Rāzī himself there says he proves only two: the **essence** and the **relation called knowing**, an aspect not identical in meaning with the essence. One who admits that God knows cannot deny the aspect by which He is called knowing; the powerful is likewise the essence which can act. Yet, al-Taftāzānī argues, knowledge cannot be **nothing but** an extrinsic relation. Al-Rāzī himself says elsewhere, in the *Nihāyat al-ʿUqūl*, that if knowledge and power were mere relations their existence would depend on the pre-existence of their relata; an object of knowledge might be impossible, and a possible effect might itself come to exist only by divine knowledge and power. One must thus not collapse the disputed **real attribute** into a subsequently established relation.
### Proofs for real affirmative attributes

**First—the analogy from the visible to the unseen.** Classical theologians reason from the sensible (*shāhid*) to the unseen (*ghāʾib*), but they require an appropriate common ground. Al-Juwaynī names four grounds: **cause** (*ʿilla*), **condition** (*sharṭ*), **reality or defining character** (*ḥaqīqa*), and **evidence/indication** (*dalīl*). If, in what is visible, the property of being-knowing has knowledge for its ground, or is conditioned by life; if the essential account of the knower is one in whom knowledge subsists; or if an effect rationally indicates its cause, then the appropriate inference can be made about the unseen. Mere observation that human agents possess bodies with spatial limits does *not* make God bodily: there is no corresponding ground for that inference. In the sensible realm, knowledge explains one's being a knower and enters the account of what it means to be such; the inference is therefore extended to the unseen divine Knower, and likewise to power and life. This works dialectically against Muʿtazilites who accept properly qualified inference from the sensible to the unseen and accept that knowledge explains being-knowing among creatures.

**Objections and answers.** In creatures, these conditions might require explanatory attributes because they are **contingent**, whereas divine knowing is necessary. Again, the visible and unseen do not have identical attributes: one is originated and bounded, the other eternal and unrestricted. The answer is that **necessity does not exclude an explanation** by what is itself necessary, and the relevant common character is knowledge insofar as it makes a knower a knower—not knowledge's being an accident, originated, limited or corporeal. The analogy thus requires identifying its true explanatory ground rather than transferring all accompanying properties.

**Second—the meaning of 'knowing' and 'powerful'.** God is knowing. In ordinary metaphysical usage the knower has knowledge; there is no intelligible account of the designation otherwise. Likewise the powerful has power, the living life. Conversely, God has objects known; what is known is precisely that to which knowledge is related. **Objection.** Even granting knowledge, why must it be **additional** to the essence rather than the essence itself? Several absurdities seem to follow from identity. Calling God knowing would provide no information, any more than saying 'human is human'. Knowledge and power and life would be **identical to one another** through identity with the same essence. It would be immediately evident without a demonstration that God is knowing and powerful, because a thing's identity with itself is self-evident. Furthermore, 'knowledge' itself would then be an intrinsically necessary existent, creator and object of worship, living, knowing and powerful—claims rejected by the opposing parties as well.

**Counter-objection.** These absurdities follow only if *identity in reality* entails *identity in conception*. Even if essence, knowing and power are identical in existence, the **meanings** of their conceptions differ: a person is a writer, laugher, knower and agent without comprising several separate substances. A predicate can convey new information while designating the same real subject. **Reply.** The argument does not concern the derived predicates 'knowing' and 'powerful', which are predicated of the subject, but the abstract grounds of derivation, **knowledge**, **power**, and **life**, whose predication of the subject is not simply univocal naming of the subject. If these are *nothing but* the subject, the problems return.

**Further counter-objection.** Could not the essence considered under one relation to things known be knowledge, and under another relation to things effected be power; and under the capacity for both be life? A single entity can be a half relative to two, a third relative to three, and a quarter relative to four, without being numerically multiplied by its many relations. **Reply.** The one number is not itself the abstract relation of **halfness** or **thirdness**. It bears those relations. Likewise the divine essence is a knower and agent, but this leaves the ground of its knowledge and power unexplained. Knowledge and power are not mere second intentions or conceptual abstractions like origination and possibility; they are real positive features. Either they reduce to the essence, with the cited consequences, or signify something over and above it. The attribution of knowing or being-able arises from the appropriate **grounds of derivation** (*maʾkhadh al-ishtiqāq*); a mere change in the language of relations does not eliminate the need to explain those grounds.

In summary, there is no dispute that God is knowing, living, and able to act. These are not bare alternative proper names for one essence. The terms express knowledge, ability to act or abstain, and other positive grounds. To be devoid of them would entail lack of knowledge or power, and therefore deficiency. Such real grounds are not themselves free-standing necessary essences; because the identity hypothesis generates the cited difficulties, they must be understood as **real attributes additional to the essence**, in the carefully qualified sense described at the beginning of the chapter. Al-Taftāzānī treats the Muʿtazilite insistence that God is knowing without knowledge and powerful without power as an implausible retreat from the ordinary implications of the terms.

**Third—scriptural evidence.** Revealed expressions affirm **knowledge** and **power** themselves, not just the derived terms knowing and powerful. The text adduces Qurʾānic phrases such as revelation 'by His knowledge' and 'the power belongs to God' and the description of God as the strong Possessor of power. These need careful grammatical interpretation—for example, a preposition must not be taken to say that the *attribute of knowledge itself* was sent down with the revelation—but they are presented as difficult to reduce to a denial of any real knowledge or power.

### Objections raised by those who deny additional attributes

Al-Taftāzānī groups opponents' proofs into several kinds. Some rely on philosophical principles, others on characteristic Muʿtazilite kalām principles, while some arise from attempts to reconcile problems internally within Sunni theology. They are not all attributed to a single author.

**First—the dependence of an additional attribute.** A divine attribute additional to the essence cannot be self-subsisting and therefore appears **possible** rather than independently necessary. Its dependence upon the divine essence would make the Necessary at once **producer and recipient**, which, the objector argues, was rejected in the discussion of causes. Statements that 'the Necessary Existent is God and His attributes' must therefore be understood, if admitted at all, to mean that the attributes are necessary **through God's essence**, not each intrinsically necessary. A distinction is sometimes made between God's freely producing created things and His eternally necessitating His attributes. But the author observes the apparent strain of introducing such restrictions into supposedly universal metaphysical judgements. The denial that producer and recipient can coincide is itself disputable; moreover, if all possible things ultimately depend upon God, that fact does not imply that He immediately produces every effect in the same way, a point which complicates an objection raised by philosophers with mediated causal chains.

**Second—the objection from divine perfection.** If an additional attribute were not a perfection it would be unworthy of God; if it were a perfection, God would be **perfected by another**, contradicting His intrinsic completeness. **Reply.** Deny that every item which is not itself a perfection is therefore a deficiency, and deny that every attribute not identical with the essence is *other* in the independent sense intended by the proof. On the theologians' view the attributes are neither simply the essence nor beings separable from it. Even if the attribute is distinct, a perfection eternally flowing from the very essence is not an externally supplied completion of a previously deficient being.

**Third—the Muʿtazilite argument from the necessity of knowing.** God's being knowing is necessary, since ignorance is impossible and He cannot need some external agent to make Him a knower. What is necessary requires no explanatory cause. Therefore divine being-knowing is not due to a further knowledge. **Reply.** Even allowing a distinct *state of knowing* grounded in the attribute of knowledge, the 'necessity' in question does not mean that the derived state is an **intrinsically necessary, self-subsisting existent**. It means that the essence cannot lack the state. An inseparable, necessary concomitant may still have an explanation in a property arising eternally from the essence.

**Fourth—the plurality of eternals, the opponents' strongest religious objection.** The attributes must either have arisen, introducing originated qualities into the divine essence and implying a previous lack of knowledge, power and life, or be eternal. If eternal, there would appear to be a multiplicity of beginningless entities, which opponents condemn by appeal to the Muslim consensus against a plurality of gods, citing the three hypostases ascribed to Christianity. **Reply.** The attributes and the essence are not 'others' in the sense of things separable in place, time, existence or nonexistence; this denies the intended multiplicity of **independent essences**. But the very word 'other' is disputed. Al-Juwaynī cautions that reason and revelation do not yield a decisive universal definition of 'otherness' that would simply rule out calling two existing things 'others'; he also freely speaks of the divine knowledge and essence as two *existents*. Thus one cannot secure the theology merely by insisting, without qualification, that no real plurality is involved. The stronger distinction is between **self-subsisting intrinsically necessary divine beings** and **eternal attributes of the one divine essence**. The author also distinguishes beginninglessness in **time**, meaning without a beginning, from priority without **dependence on another**, meaning intrinsic necessity. Christian trinitarian claims as described in the source are not equivalent to one necessary God with eternal attributes, and the text adduces Qurʾānic condemnation of 'three' as concerning a plurality in divinity, not an arbitrary count of attributes.

### Other attempted objections

A further argument claims that the divine essence would be **composite of essence and attributes**, thus contingent. The answer denies that the essence itself is made *out of* its properties. Another says that beginninglessness is the most specific, reality-disclosing property of God; if the attributes share it, they share divinity. The reply says that it is **necessity through itself**, not mere temporal beginninglessness, which has the relevant exclusive status. Another alleges an absence of any proof for extra attributes; the reply denies the premise, referring to rational and revealed indications already given. Yet another reduces the subsistence of attributes to physical or spatial **inherence**, incompatible with divine transcendence. The reply is that the relevant subsistence is the **qualifying attachment** (*ikhtiṣāṣ nāʿit*) by which God is knowing and powerful, precisely the kind of attribution opponents themselves need when they say that knowing or capable-making states belong to Him.

### The objection concerning the persistence of attributes

An especially forceful dialectical objection, though based upon the theologians' own disputed premises, concerns **persistence** (*baqāʾ*). If eternal attributes endure, and persistence is itself an additional attribute subsisting in what persists, then **an accident or qualifying meaning would subsist in another meaning** (*qiyām al-maʿnā bi-l-maʿnā*). Many theologians refuse this, as they refuse one accident's inhering in another.

Different replies have been offered. Some deny that persistence is additional: it is simply **continuance of existence**. Others allow one meaning to subsist in another when the subject is immaterial, holding that the original impossibility concerns one spatially dependent **accident in another**, because neither has independent spatial location. Others decline to predicate persistence of attributes and say only 'God persists with His attributes'; this is criticized as extremely weak, since attributes existing without beginning or end necessarily endure, regardless of verbal avoidance. Another says that **one persistence belonging to the essence** also makes the inseparable attributes persist. But why should persistence of the essence automatically be persistence of what, although inseparable, is not identical with it? The fact that one divine attribute is not simply another—knowledge is not life or power—indicates that inseparability alone cannot perform this explanatory work.

A final approach holds that an attribute **persists through itself**: the very knowledge by which God is knowing is, under another consideration, the source of its own continuance, somewhat as an individual spatial state has its own actuality. It is replied that this confuses the formal grounds of attribution: a thing is knowing *through knowledge*, capable *through power*, and persisting *through persistence*. One may distinguish the relation in which the essence is knowing from the relation in which a given attribute persists, yet then the original claim that persistence is always an additional property subsisting in another thing has been qualified. More pointedly, if an attribute may possess the feature of **persistence** through its own reality despite the conceptual difference between knowledge and persistence, why cannot the divine essence itself be knowledge and power in reality while these remain conceptually different? The argument threatens to reopen exactly the objection the attribute-realists sought to overcome.

### Particular Muʿtazilite arguments against divine power and knowledge

Regarding **power**, Muʿtazilites argue that if God possessed a distinct *power*, it would be unfit to produce bodies, since created powers cannot produce bodies. Either divine power is similar to the created powers, and like powers have like limits, or it differs from them; the difference cannot, it is claimed, be more radical than the differences among created powers themselves, none of which can produce a body. **Reply.** A common incapacity of created powers does not prove one shared explanatory cause: different things may share a consequence for different reasons. Their special limited constitutions could each explain the incapacity. Even if one common cause is required, it could be more specific than the mere **concept of power**, common to created powers but not to the divine attribute. Divine power might have a distinctive character unmatched by any created instance, and for that reason produce bodies where they cannot.

Against divine **knowledge**, three arguments are reported. **First**, if knowledge were a real divine attribute, then divine and human knowledge of the same object would have the same relation and therefore be alike: divine knowledge would become originated or ours would become beginningless. **Reply.** Sharing a relation to an object does not prove identity of the related properties, nor must alike instances agree in temporality merely by possessing a certain common aspect. **Second**, God knows infinitely many objects; if each knowledge relates to only one object, there would be infinitely many distinct knowledges, which is said to be impossible because an actually existing multitude must be finite. Why should one knowledge not concern several objects? The opponent responds that we can know God's knowing one thing without attending to His knowing another, and that our knowledge of white and black differs. But lack of attention may concern the **different relations to objects**, not numerically distinct attributes. Even if human acts of knowing differ individually, one divine knowledge could cover infinitely many objects. This does not imply that one divine property can substitute indiscriminately for *knowledge, power and life*, whose specific kinds differ. **Third**, the Qurʾānic statement 'above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows' is said to imply a knower above God if He were the bearer of knowledge; the reply denies that the statement must be applied without qualification to God, and appeals to the scriptural texts affirming His knowledge directly.

**Editorial note.** The Arabic text is rich in speaker transitions and technical qualifications. In particular (a) 'eternal', 'beginningless', and 'intrinsically necessary' are not freely interchangeable; (b) *ghayriyya* (real otherness) is not established by every conceptual distinction; and (c) a property, its relational *taʿalluq*, and the denomination it causes must be kept distinct. This is a full-interval **first-pass explanatory English rendering**, not a printed-edition verified clause-for-clause translation.
