The analogy thus requires identifying its true explanatory ground rather than transferring all accompanying properties.

Second—the meaning of 'knowing' and 'powerful'. God is knowing. In ordinary metaphysical usage the knower has knowledge; there is no intelligible account of the designation otherwise. Likewise the powerful has power, the living life. Conversely, God has objects known; what is known is precisely that to which knowledge is related. Objection. Even granting knowledge, why must it be additional to the essence rather than the essence itself? Several absurdities seem to follow from identity. Calling God knowing would provide no information, any more than saying 'human is human'. Knowledge and power and life would be identical to one another through identity with the same essence. It would be immediately evident without a demonstration that God is knowing and powerful, because a thing's identity with itself is self-evident. Furthermore, 'knowledge' itself would then be an intrinsically necessary existent, creator and object of worship, living, knowing and powerful—claims rejected by the opposing parties as well.

Counter-objection. These absurdities follow only if identity in reality entails identity in conception. Even if essence, knowing and power are identical in existence, the meanings of their conceptions differ: a person is a writer, laugher, knower and agent without comprising several separate substances. A predicate can convey new information while designating the same real subject. Reply. The argument does not concern the derived predicates 'knowing' and 'powerful', which are predicated of the subject, but the abstract grounds of derivation, knowledge, power, and life, whose predication of the subject is not simply univocal naming of the subject. If these are nothing but the subject, the problems return.

Further counter-objection. Could not the essence considered under one relation to things known be knowledge, and under another relation to things effected be power; and under the capacity for both be life? A single entity can be a half relative to two, a third relative to three, and a quarter relative to four, without being numerically multiplied by its many relations. Reply. The one number is not itself the abstract relation of halfness or thirdness. It bears those relations. Likewise the divine essence is a knower and agent, but this leaves the ground of its knowledge and power unexplained. Knowledge and power are not mere second intentions or conceptual abstractions like origination and possibility; they are real positive features. Either they reduce to the essence, with the cited consequences, or signify something over and above it. The attribution of knowing or being-able arises from the appropriate grounds of derivation (maʾkhadh al-ishtiqāq); a mere change in the language of relations does not eliminate the need to explain those grounds.

In summary, there is no dispute that God is knowing, living, and able to act. These are not bare alternative proper names for one essence. The terms express knowledge, ability to act or abstain, and other positive grounds. To be devoid of them would entail lack of knowledge or power, and therefore deficiency. Such real grounds are not themselves free-standing necessary essences; because the identity hypothesis generates the cited difficulties, they must be understood as real attributes additional to the essence, in the carefully qualified sense described at the beginning of the chapter. Al-Taftāzānī treats the Muʿtazilite insistence that God is knowing without knowledge and powerful without power as an implausible retreat from the ordinary implications of the terms.

Third—scriptural evidence. Revealed expressions affirm knowledge and power themselves, not just the derived terms knowing and powerful. The text adduces Qurʾānic phrases such as revelation 'by His knowledge' and 'the power belongs to God' and the description of God as the strong Possessor of power. These need careful grammatical interpretation—for example, a preposition must not be taken to say that the attribute of knowledge itself was sent down with the revelation—but they are presented as difficult to reduce to a denial of any real knowledge or power.

Objections raised by those who deny additional attributes

Al-Taftāzānī groups opponents' proofs into several kinds. Some rely on philosophical principles, others on characteristic Muʿtazilite kalām principles, while some arise from attempts to reconcile problems internally within Sunni theology. They are not all attributed to a single author.

First—the dependence of an additional attribute. A divine attribute additional to the essence cannot be self-subsisting and therefore appears possible rather than independently necessary. Its dependence upon the divine essence would make the Necessary at once producer and recipient, which, the objector argues, was rejected in the discussion of causes. Statements that 'the Necessary Existent is God and His attributes' must therefore be understood, if admitted at all, to mean that the attributes are necessary through God's essence, not each intrinsically necessary. A distinction is sometimes made between God's freely producing created things and His eternally necessitating His attributes. But the author observes the apparent strain of introducing such restrictions into supposedly universal metaphysical judgements. The denial that producer and recipient can coincide is itself disputable; moreover, if all possible things ultimately depend upon God, that fact does not imply that He immediately produces every effect in the same way, a point which complicates an objection raised by philosophers with mediated causal chains.

Second—the objection from divine perfection. If an additional attribute were not a perfection it would be unworthy of God; if it were a perfection, God would be perfected by another, contradicting His intrinsic completeness. Reply. Deny that every item which is not itself a perfection is therefore a deficiency, and deny that every attribute not identical with the essence is other in the independent sense intended by the proof. On the theologians' view the attributes are neither simply the essence nor beings separable from it. Even if the attribute is distinct, a perfection eternally flowing from the very essence is not an externally supplied completion of a previously deficient being.

Third—the Muʿtazilite argument from the necessity of knowing. God's being knowing is necessary, since ignorance is impossible and He cannot need some external agent to make Him a knower. What is necessary requires no explanatory cause. Therefore divine being-knowing is not due to a further knowledge. Reply. Even allowing a distinct state of knowing grounded in the attribute of knowledge, the 'necessity' in question does not mean that the derived state is an intrinsically necessary, self-subsisting existent. It means that the essence cannot lack the state. An inseparable, necessary concomitant may still have an explanation in a property arising eternally from the essence.

Fourth—the plurality of eternals, the opponents' strongest religious objection. The attributes must either have arisen, introducing originated qualities into the divine essence and implying a previous lack of knowledge, power and life, or be eternal. If eternal, there would appear to be a multiplicity of beginningless entities, which opponents condemn by appeal to the Muslim consensus against a plurality of gods, citing the three hypostases ascribed to Christianity. Reply. The attributes and the essence are not 'others' in the sense of things separable in place, time, existence or nonexistence; this denies the intended multiplicity of independent essences. But the very word 'other' is disputed. Al-Juwaynī cautions that reason and revelation do not yield a decisive universal definition of 'otherness' that would simply rule out calling two existing things 'others'; he also freely speaks of the divine knowledge and essence as two existents. Thus one cannot secure the theology merely by insisting, without qualification, that no real plurality is involved. The stronger distinction is between self-subsisting intrinsically necessary divine beings and eternal attributes of the one divine essence. The author also distinguishes beginninglessness in time, meaning without a beginning, from priority without dependence on another, meaning intrinsic necessity. Christian trinitarian claims as described in the source are not equivalent to one necessary God with eternal attributes, and the text adduces Qurʾānic condemnation of 'three' as concerning a plurality in divinity, not an arbitrary count of attributes.

Other attempted objections

A further argument claims that the divine essence would be composite of essence and attributes, thus contingent. The answer denies that the essence itself is made out of its properties. Another says that beginninglessness is the most specific, reality-disclosing property of God; if the attributes share it, they share divinity. The reply says that it is necessity through itself, not mere temporal beginninglessness, which has the relevant exclusive status. Another alleges an absence of any proof for extra attributes; the reply denies the premise, referring to rational and revealed indications already given. Yet another reduces the subsistence of attributes to physical or spatial inherence, incompatible with divine transcendence. The reply is that the relevant subsistence is the qualifying attachment (ikhtiṣāṣ nāʿit) by which God is knowing and powerful, precisely the kind of attribution opponents themselves need when they say that knowing or capable-making states belong to Him.

The objection concerning the persistence of attributes

An especially forceful dialectical objection, though based upon the theologians' own disputed premises, concerns persistence (baqāʾ). If eternal attributes endure, and persistence is itself an additional attribute subsisting in what persists, then an accident or qualifying meaning would subsist in another meaning (qiyām al-maʿnā bi-l-maʿnā). Many theologians refuse this, as they refuse one accident's inhering in another.

Different replies have been offered. Some deny that persistence is additional: it is simply continuance of existence. Others allow one meaning to subsist in another when the subject is immaterial, holding that the original impossibility concerns one spatially dependent accident in another, because neither has independent spatial location. Others decline to predicate persistence of attributes and say only 'God persists with His attributes'; this is criticized as extremely weak, since attributes existing without beginning or end necessarily endure, regardless of verbal avoidance. Another says that one persistence belonging to the essence also makes the inseparable attributes persist. But why should persistence of the essence automatically be persistence of what, although inseparable, is not identical with it? The fact that one divine attribute is not simply another—knowledge is not life or power—indicates that inseparability alone cannot perform this explanatory work.

A final approach holds that an attribute persists through itself: the very knowledge by which God is knowing is, under another consideration, the source of its own continuance, somewhat as an individual spatial state has its own actuality. It is replied that this confuses the formal grounds of attribution: a thing is knowing through knowledge, capable through power, and persisting through persistence. One may distinguish the relation in which the essence is knowing from the relation in which a given attribute persists, yet then the original claim that persistence is always an additional property subsisting in another thing has been qualified. More pointedly, if an attribute may possess the feature of persistence through its own reality despite the conceptual difference between knowledge and persistence, why cannot the divine essence itself be knowledge and power in reality while these remain conceptually different? The argument threatens to reopen exactly the objection the attribute-realists sought to overcome.

Particular Muʿtazilite arguments against divine power and knowledge

Regarding power, Muʿtazilites argue that if God possessed a distinct power, it would be unfit to produce bodies, since created powers cannot produce bodies. Either divine power is similar to the created powers, and like powers have like limits, or it differs from them; the difference cannot, it is claimed, be more radical than the differences among created powers themselves, none of which can produce a body. Reply. A common incapacity of created powers does not prove one shared explanatory cause: different things may share a consequence for different reasons. Their special limited constitutions could each explain the incapacity. Even if one common cause is required, it could be more specific than the mere concept of power, common to created powers but not to the divine attribute. Divine power might have a distinctive character unmatched by any created instance, and for that reason produce bodies where they cannot.

Against divine knowledge, three arguments are reported. First, if knowledge were a real divine attribute, then divine and human knowledge of the same object would have the same relation and therefore be alike: divine knowledge would become originated or ours would become beginningless. Reply. Sharing a relation to an object does not prove identity of the related properties, nor must alike instances agree in temporality merely by possessing a certain common aspect. Second, God knows infinitely many objects; if each knowledge relates to only one object, there would be infinitely many distinct knowledges, which is said to be impossible because an actually existing multitude must be finite. Why should one knowledge not concern several objects? The opponent responds that we can know God's knowing one thing without attending to His knowing another, and that our knowledge of white and black differs. But lack of attention may concern the different relations to objects, not numerically distinct attributes. Even if human acts of knowing differ individually, one divine knowledge could cover infinitely many objects. This does not imply that one divine property can substitute indiscriminately for knowledge, power and life, whose specific kinds differ. Third, the Qurʾānic statement 'above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows' is said to imply a knower above God if He were the bearer of knowledge; the reply denies that the statement must be applied without qualification to God, and appeals to the scriptural texts affirming His knowledge directly.

Editorial note. The Arabic text is rich in speaker transitions and technical qualifications. In particular (a) 'eternal', 'beginningless', and 'intrinsically necessary' are not freely interchangeable; (b) ghayriyya (real otherness) is not established by every conceptual distinction; and (c) a property, its relational taʿalluq, and the denomination it causes must be kept distinct. This is a full-interval first-pass explanatory English rendering, not a printed-edition verified clause-for-clause translation.

title: Divine power (*qudra*): freedom, necessity, the scope of power and created agency

**Source:** *Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid*, electronic vol. II, pp. 78–86, canonical characters 1094493–1111875 (exclusive). **Status:** new source-ordered close explanatory translation, not yet checked line by line against print.

### The meaning of being powerful

**“The second investigation concerns His being powerful.”** The familiar definition of the **capable agent** (*al-qādir*) is one who **acts if he wills and refrains if he wills**. That is, both acting and refraining are possible from him according to differing motivations. This does not exclude an action's becoming necessary once the motive has become decisive, so that under those circumstances its not occurring is impossible. Nor does this obliterate the difference between a capable agent and an **agent necessitating by its essence** (*mūjib*). The latter produces its effect in view of its essence in such a way that it is altogether unable to refrain; “if it willed to refrain, it would refrain” is not true of it. The sun's illumination and fire's heating serve as examples of necessitating natural action.

Al-Rāzī inclines toward classifying the **motive** (*dāʿī*) as a kind of cognition: knowledge, opinion, or belief that an action contains benefit or advantage. Others classify the motive as a kind of will, and yet others identify it with the benefit or advantage itself. There is plainly no necessity that the benefit really exist in the object: a person may mistakenly take harm for benefit and proceed to act on that belief.

### An originated effect from an eternal agent

The principal proof used for God's being capable is that He is a **beginningless Maker** whose work is originated. An originated product can proceed from a beginningless Maker only by **power**, not by automatic necessitation; otherwise the effect would fail to accompany its **complete cause** (*al-ʿilla al-tāmma*), for the supposed cause was present from eternity while the effect was not. The inference needs a further premise: some originated thing must be traced to God **without an intermediate cause**. The theologians establish that through the beginninglessness of God and His attributes and the origination of the entire world. Alternatively, they must eliminate a chain in which the original Necessary Existent produces a beginningless **free agent** who produces originated things, or a beginningless **motion** whose continually new parts supply the conditions and preparations for generated events. The philosophers propose precisely such alternatives.

The earlier discussions of infinite regress and the origination of the world are therefore presupposed. In particular, al-Taftāzānī recalls the theologians' denial of a beginningless succession of generated events, whether simultaneous or successive. Al-Juwaynī calls an endless series of successive originated occurrences intrinsically repugnant to the first judgements of reason. How could one-by-one events already have elapsed when their number had **no beginning**? On the philosophers' account, before this celestial revolution there was another without first revolution; likewise parent before child, seed before crop, and chicken before egg. By contrast, events having **no final member**, as in eternal blessedness, do not involve an already completed infinite preceding sequence. The analogy is with the conditions “I will give you a dirham only after I have given you a dinar, and a dinar only after a dirham”: no payment can start. This differs from promising a dirham followed by a dinar followed by a dirham indefinitely. Origination excludes an absolutely beginningless past but does not, by that fact alone, exclude an endless future.

**Objection:** May one not formulate the proof without either supplementary premise? As *al-Mawāqif* proposes, without a powerful agent there would be no originated event, or there would be an uncaused event, or an infinite causal regress, or an effect delayed behind its complete cause. If an originated event exists, it has a cause; the cause must terminate in something beginningless; the beginningless cause must, supposedly, produce an originated effect immediately. **Reply:** This is only the earlier argument with superfluous conditional steps added. Its real difficulty remains. One still needs to exclude an eternal necessitating source that produces an **eternal free intermediary**, or originated movements extending without beginning whose parts mediate the occurrence of events. This second kind of regress—each originated event preceded by another—is not identical to an endless series of simultaneous dependent causes. The relevant alternative must be independently ruled out.

### Six demonstrations for freedom and power

Al-Taftāzānī then reviews six formulations by the theologians.

**First**, because all originated things terminate at the Necessary Existent, as demonstrated in the proofs of the Maker and the refutation of regress, He must be powerful and able to choose. Otherwise He either necessarily produces an originated thing immediately, making the effect fail to accompany its beginningless complete cause, or each originated thing is preceded by another without beginning. Both alternatives were rejected.

**Second**, God's production of the world must be by power and choice. If it were through necessitation, it would be either without intermediary or by an eternal intermediary, making the world eternal; or it would occur by an originated intermediary, reopening the same question of its origin and giving an endless succession of originated intermediaries.

**Third**, the differences in bodies—the particular colour, figure, taste, smell and other determinations assigned to each—require a **specifier** (*mukhaṣṣiṣ*), since the occurrence of a determinate alternative without something specifying it is impossible. Bodyhood itself cannot provide the specification because it is common to the bodies. The required additional specifier either leads to an unacceptable regress of specifiers or ends in a capable agent acting by choice. A natural necessitating cause, as such, relates equally to the alternatives needing specification.

**Fourth**, if God's production of the world were necessary through His essence, the nonexistence of the world would indicate the nonexistence of God, for the absence of an inseparable consequent indicates the absence of its antecedent. But the Necessary Existent's absence is impossible. Therefore His production is by power and choice rather than intrinsic necessitation. This formulation is part of the dialectic and must be read alongside the dependence of the conclusion on the world's origination.

**Fifth**, the assignment of stars and poles to their determinate places needs a capable chooser. If a necessitating agent without choice performed it, an alternative would be preferred without a preferent, since all regions of the simple heaven are alike in relation to such an agent.

**Sixth**, the maker of a living creature and its organs, with their differentiated configurations, must possess power and choice. Were generation the necessary effect of the nature of the reproductive fluid or of an external necessitating cause, a simple fluid would yield a spherical organism, since a uniform nature relates uniformly to all directions. If composed of simple bodies it would produce juxtaposed spheres, not the differentiated organic structure observed.

Other arguments invoke consensus and decisive scriptural passages; the status of knowledge, power and life as perfections incompatible with ignorance, incapacity and death; and the manifest intricacy, order and fitness of the heavens and earth. Al-Taftāzānī notes points open to challenge: scriptural evidence itself depends on the authority of revelation and miracles, and whether power is an intrinsic perfection of the Necessary must not merely be presumed. A demonstration from fine workmanship must also exclude the philosopher's hypothesis that the immediate producer is an intermediary emanating from God. Yet the seeker seriously attentive to truth may attain firm conviction through these arguments even where a disputant can raise technical objections.

### Seven objections to a freely acting Necessary Existent

**First objection:** If God's power chooses one of two alternatives equally possible to it, a **preferent** is required, leading to a regress of preferents, or is not required, apparently destroying the argument for a Maker, which depends on the impossibility of a possible occurrence without a preferent. **Reply:** Neither inference is conceded. The preferent may be **will itself**, whose function is to select one of equal alternatives without another selector, like the hungry person choosing one of two loaves or a fleeing person one of two roads. This is preferable to saying that power as such chooses an alternative by its own essence. Nor does the permission for a **capable agent to choose** without an additional desire imply that an existent effect can come to be **without any efficient source**. The senses of “without a preferent” differ between these cases.

**Second objection:** If the eternal power and will eternally relate to bringing the world into existence, the world must be eternal, since a complete cause cannot be delayed from its effect. If the relation is originated, its origination requires a further relation, and so infinitely. **Reply:** An eternal will can intend from eternity that the world exist **at a future time**. A new relation of power or will need not be created by another relation: its occurrence can follow from the attribute itself. In addition, *taʿalluqāt*, relations of an attribute to its object, are intellectual considerations, and the alleged regress terminates when the consideration terminates.

**Third objection:** If every positive and negative condition necessary for the effect is present, the effect must follow and the agent cannot refrain; if some condition is absent, the effect cannot occur. There is thus supposedly no difference between an agent acting by choice and one necessitating by its essence. **Reply:** Even conceding that no effect can be absent when the free agent's total conditions are complete, this does not make him a necessitating cause in the disputed sense. **Necessity consequent upon free choice confirms rather than abolishes choice.** If he willed to refrain, he could refrain, unlike the intrinsically necessitating agent.

**Fourth objection:** Power must relate equally to the **existence** and **nonexistence** of its object. But original nonexistence is beginningless and cannot be an effect of a capable agent; it is mere negation, not something upon which power can work. **Reply:** Saying nonexistence lies within power means that, if the agent wills **not to produce** something, it does not produce it; or if it does not will its production, it does not produce it. The incoherent claim would be that it *produces nonexistence as a positive effect*. The argument concerns the nature of power in any agent, not God alone.

**Fifth objection:** If God's action is preferable **for Himself** to refraining, He acquires perfection through another; if it is not preferable, the action is frivolous. Neither suits the Necessary. **Reply:** An action can be preferable **in itself** or **for another** without improving its agent. Even if what does not benefit its agent is defined as frivolous, the further claim that every such action is impossible for God needs proof.

**Sixth objection:** Freedom would make the impossible possible, or allow the beginningless to be an effect of power. If the effect was impossible in eternity but later possible, impossibility has turned into possibility. If it was already possible in eternity, then by being attributed to a capable agent it seems possible for a beginningless thing to be an effect. **Reply:** Something can be possible **in itself** even when its occurrence in eternity **under the description of an originated effect** is impossible. One cannot infer that power can produce a beginningless effect from the intrinsic possibility of the essence of an effect at all times.

**Seventh objection:** God's eternal knowledge determines whether an effect will occur. If He knows it will occur, the occurrence is necessary; if He knows it will not, it is impossible. Neither necessaries nor impossibilities can be objects of power, since the capacity to do otherwise is lost. **Reply:** God knows that the effect will occur **through His power**. A necessity consequent upon such a free act does not destroy its being within power; it presupposes and confirms it.

### The infinity and universality of divine power

**Conclusion.** Divine power is infinite. If this means it has no extended nature that could reach a physical boundary, or that it never ceases to exist, the claim is straightforward. If it means that there is **no final limit of possibility** beyond which it becomes unable to relate to another possible object, this follows because such failure would be incapacity and defect. Many divine effects may themselves endure without end, such as the bliss of Paradise, whose successive instances are endless in possibility. The ground of God's being capable is His essence; the ground of an object being capable of receiving power's operation is its **possibility**. Neither ground terminates at some further possible thing.

This last argument is invoked for the universality of power over all possible beings. An objection observes that being possible does not by itself show that an object meets all the *conditions* for the attachment of power or lacks all *impediments*. A suggested answer denies there are differences among possible things before existence sufficient to distinguish their conditions; the author regards this as weak. The stronger appeal is to revealed statements of the universality of divine power, such as “God is powerful over all things.”

### Disagreements about universality

The source reviews schools said to restrict the objects of divine power. The **Majūs** are represented as attributing evil and noxious things to another agent, Ahriman, in order to avoid making one ultimate being both good and evil. **Al-Naẓẓām and his adherents** are said to hold that God cannot create ignorance, falsehood, injustice and other ugly acts: if able to create them He could perform them, but their performance would imply folly if their ugliness were known, or ignorance if it were not. **Reply:** That a thing is ugly *in relation to God* is denied. Even if conceded, the ability to do it is compatible with the impossibility of its occurrence because the relevant motives are absent or countervailing reasons present. **ʿAbbād and his followers** deny God's ability to do what He knows will not occur, since its occurrence would be impossible; another report extends this to what He knows will occur, since its occurrence is necessary. The reply reprises the distinction of **conditioned necessity** from intrinsic impossibility of being an object of power.

**Al-Kaʿbī and his adherents** deny that God can produce an act **similar to** one within a servant's power; otherwise the same movement caused by God and by a servant would have to be alike. Their argument appeals to the supposition that a servant's act must be obedience, folly or humility (or, in variant summaries, obedience, disobedience and folly), descriptions they deny of divine acts. The proposed exhaustive disjunction is rejected: acts can pursue ordinary worldly benefit without being obedience or humility, which specifically include submission or reverence to another. Moreover, the intrinsic object of power is a **movement or rest**; the moral or intentional descriptions attend it in virtue of the servant's aims and motives and do not constitute an essential difference in the movement itself.

**Al-Jubbāʾī and his followers** deny that God can produce **the very same individual effect** within a servant's power, lest one effect be created by two creators, because a complete motive and power would make it occur through each. **Reply on the theologians' account:** The servant's power is not, in the relevant sense, an independent producer. Even conceding some efficiency to it, the presence of one agent's power or will might prevent the completion of the other's conditions. And even if both co-operated, the effect could be attributed **to their joint agency**, rather than independently to each. Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī offers the example of a single body connected to two people, one pulling and another pushing, with the resulting motion attributed to both; the author remarks that this requires scrutiny.

A crucial **threefold distinction of “universality”** now follows. (1) God is capable of **every possible thing**, whether or not that thing is ever willed or produced by Him or whether some created power is said to produce it. The foregoing controversies primarily concern this sense. (2) Every actually existing possible thing depends on God **directly or through intermediaries**. Monotheists agreeing upon one Necessary Existent do not ordinarily contest this abstract dependency, although they dispute the mediators and precise dependency relations. (3) All beings **other than God's essence and attributes** exist **immediately by His power and will**, with no other efficient producer. This is the stronger account adopted by certain Sunni theologians, including Ashʿarīs; it must not be confused with the previous two.

Defenders of (3) adduce scriptural language that God alone is the Creator and in particular creates heaven and earth, darkness and light, death and life, substances and accidents. Their **proof from concurrence of independent powers** (*tawārud*) argues that if another power produces a thing which lies also within God's power, and the two wills simultaneously determine the one effect, then production by one rather than the other is an arbitrary preference without a preferent; production independently by both would make one effect depend on **two separately sufficient causes**. In the case of two persons pushing or pulling one body, however, neither individual is proved independently sufficient to produce *that determinate motion*. A possible rejoinder is that divine power is the stronger of the two, and the created power is thereby ineffective.

The **proof from mutual hindrance** (*tamānuʿ*) assumes God's will and an alleged independent creator's will simultaneously determine **opposites**, such as motion and rest of one body at one time. If both happen, opposites coexist; if neither happens, God's power is frustrated and the body lacks both motion and rest; if one happens, there is allegedly a preference without a preferent. An opponent may answer that divine power is **more perfect**. This need not mean merely that it operates on more kinds of objects, while its influence on this particular object is equal. It may mean **greater efficacy in the very act**, such that divine power prevails and the creature's supposed power fails.

### Positions of philosophers and other groups

The claim that God alone is the immediate effective cause of every existence is characteristic of some Sunni theologians, while numerous other groups differ. The **philosophers** say the first immediate effect of the Necessary is a separate intellect, from which follow an intellect, a soul and a celestial sphere in successive orders. Intellects produce the spheres; souls produce their movements; terrestrial occurrences arise through their principles, substantial forms, powers, and the mediation of celestial movements. Particular forms explain the operations of minerals, and souls those of plants and animals. Many possible beings thus possess efficiency in their account.

The **astral determinists and astrologers** attribute sublunary changes to the states, positions, movements and conjunctions of the heavenly bodies. Their principal inference is from observed **concomitant variation** (*dawarān*) of phenomena with celestial states. This does not conclusively prove causality: the celestial conditions could be instruments, prerequisites or simultaneous results. Miracles and extraordinary occurrences are also offered against rigid predictions. The school additionally assumes heavenly simplicity and regularity while introducing sharply differing qualities and dominions of signs, degrees and planets. The **naturalists** likewise infer from correlations that terrestrial occurrences proceed through the mixtures, powers and qualities of elements. Al-Taftāzānī notes that these views may be classified under philosophy, but are separately attributed because their advocates' positions on the first principles—separate intellects, celestial souls, whether God chooses, and so on—may be unknown.

Among Muslims the **Muʿtazilites** attribute voluntary deeds to human and animal agents; the case is developed in the later discussion of the **creation of acts**. The source also groups with them certain explanations of evil acts by the devil, a polemical comparison requiring particular care in historical attribution.

**Final terminological qualification.** An objection asks why philosophers who deny God's action through free power are included among deniers of its *universality* rather than deniers of power altogether. Here “power” sometimes means simply **being capable** (*qādiriyya*). The philosophers can use an account on which a capable agent is one from whom an action could or could not issue, with will or its absence determining the issue and the action necessarily following when will is present. Their will is treated as a specific knowledge, and their knowledge and power are beginningless and not really additional to the essence. Under this formulation they nevertheless maintain an eternal world and a Maker necessitating through His essence. Al-Taftāzānī's judgment is that **this preserves the words ‘power’ and ‘will’ but not the intended freedom they signify**.

**Textual and doctrinal cautions:** Some terms and punctuation are introduced to make the dialectical progression readable. The six proofs, seven counterarguments, three senses of universality, and several school attributions should be checked against printed pages and any variant critical editions before publication. The model of free agency must not be reduced either to bare chance or to necessitating action independent of will.

This does not exclude an action's becoming necessary once the motive has become decisive, so that under those circumstances its not occurring is impossible. Nor does this obliterate the difference between a capable agent and an agent necessitating by its essence (mūjib). The latter produces its effect in view of its essence in such a way that it is altogether unable to refrain; “if it willed to refrain, it would refrain” is not true of it. The sun's illumination and fire's heating serve as examples of necessitating natural action.

Al-Rāzī inclines toward classifying the motive (dāʿī) as a kind of cognition: knowledge, opinion, or belief that an action contains benefit or advantage. Others classify the motive as a kind of will, and yet others identify it with the benefit or advantage itself. There is plainly no necessity that the benefit really exist in the object: a person may mistakenly take harm for benefit and proceed to act on that belief.

An originated effect from an eternal agent

The principal proof used for God's being capable is that He is a beginningless Maker whose work is originated. An originated product can proceed from a beginningless Maker only by power, not by automatic necessitation; otherwise the effect would fail to accompany its complete cause (al-ʿilla al-tāmma), for the supposed cause was present from eternity while the effect was not. The inference needs a further premise: some originated thing must be traced to God without an intermediate cause. The theologians establish that through the beginninglessness of God and His attributes and the origination of the entire world. Alternatively, they must eliminate a chain in which the original Necessary Existent produces a beginningless free agent who produces originated things, or a beginningless motion whose continually new parts supply the conditions and preparations for generated events. The philosophers propose precisely such alternatives.

The earlier discussions of infinite regress and the origination of the world are therefore presupposed. In particular, al-Taftāzānī recalls the theologians' denial of a beginningless succession of generated events, whether simultaneous or successive. Al-Juwaynī calls an endless series of successive originated occurrences intrinsically repugnant to the first judgements of reason. How could one-by-one events already have elapsed when their number had no beginning? On the philosophers' account, before this celestial revolution there was another without first revolution; likewise parent before child, seed before crop, and chicken before egg. By contrast, events having no final member, as in eternal blessedness, do not involve an already completed infinite preceding sequence. The analogy is with the conditions “I will give you a dirham only after I have given you a dinar, and a dinar only after a dirham”: no payment can start. This differs from promising a dirham followed by a dinar followed by a dirham indefinitely. Origination excludes an absolutely beginningless past but does not, by that fact alone, exclude an endless future.

Objection: May one not formulate the proof without either supplementary premise? As al-Mawāqif proposes, without a powerful agent there would be no originated event, or there would be an uncaused event, or an infinite causal regress, or an effect delayed behind its complete cause. If an originated event exists, it has a cause; the cause must terminate in something beginningless; the beginningless cause must, supposedly, produce an originated effect immediately. Reply: This is only the earlier argument with superfluous conditional steps added. Its real difficulty remains. One still needs to exclude an eternal necessitating source that produces an eternal free intermediary, or originated movements extending without beginning whose parts mediate the occurrence of events. This second kind of regress—each originated event preceded by another—is not identical to an endless series of simultaneous dependent causes. The relevant alternative must be independently ruled out.

Six demonstrations for freedom and power

Al-Taftāzānī then reviews six formulations by the theologians.

First, because all originated things terminate at the Necessary Existent, as demonstrated in the proofs of the Maker and the refutation of regress, He must be powerful and able to choose. Otherwise He either necessarily produces an originated thing immediately, making the effect fail to accompany its beginningless complete cause, or each originated thing is preceded by another without beginning. Both alternatives were rejected.

Second, God's production of the world must be by power and choice. If it were through necessitation, it would be either without intermediary or by an eternal intermediary, making the world eternal; or it would occur by an originated intermediary, reopening the same question of its origin and giving an endless succession of originated intermediaries.

Third, the differences in bodies—the particular colour, figure, taste, smell and other determinations assigned to each—require a specifier (mukhaṣṣiṣ), since the occurrence of a determinate alternative without something specifying it is impossible. Bodyhood itself cannot provide the specification because it is common to the bodies. The required additional specifier either leads to an unacceptable regress of specifiers or ends in a capable agent acting by choice. A natural necessitating cause, as such, relates equally to the alternatives needing specification.

Fourth, if God's production of the world were necessary through His essence, the nonexistence of the world would indicate the nonexistence of God, for the absence of an inseparable consequent indicates the absence of its antecedent. But the Necessary Existent's absence is impossible. Therefore His production is by power and choice rather than intrinsic necessitation. This formulation is part of the dialectic and must be read alongside the dependence of the conclusion on the world's origination.

Fifth, the assignment of stars and poles to their determinate places needs a capable chooser. If a necessitating agent without choice performed it, an alternative would be preferred without a preferent, since all regions of the simple heaven are alike in relation to such an agent.

Sixth, the maker of a living creature and its organs, with their differentiated configurations, must possess power and choice. Were generation the necessary effect of the nature of the reproductive fluid or of an external necessitating cause, a simple fluid would yield a spherical organism, since a uniform nature relates uniformly to all directions. If composed of simple bodies it would produce juxtaposed spheres, not the differentiated organic structure observed.

Other arguments invoke consensus and decisive scriptural passages; the status of knowledge, power and life as perfections incompatible with ignorance, incapacity and death; and the manifest intricacy, order and fitness of the heavens and earth. Al-Taftāzānī notes points open to challenge: scriptural evidence itself depends on the authority of revelation and miracles, and whether power is an intrinsic perfection of the Necessary must not merely be presumed. A demonstration from fine workmanship must also exclude the philosopher's hypothesis that the immediate producer is an intermediary emanating from God. Yet the seeker seriously attentive to truth may attain firm conviction through these arguments even where a disputant can raise technical objections.

Seven objections to a freely acting Necessary Existent

First objection: If God's power chooses one of two alternatives equally possible to it, a preferent is required, leading to a regress of preferents, or is not required, apparently destroying the argument for a Maker, which depends on the impossibility of a possible occurrence without a preferent. Reply: Neither inference is conceded. The preferent may be will itself, whose function is to select one of equal alternatives without another selector, like the hungry person choosing one of two loaves or a fleeing person one of two roads. This is preferable to saying that power as such chooses an alternative by its own essence. Nor does the permission for a capable agent to choose without an additional desire imply that an existent effect can come to be without any efficient source. The senses of “without a preferent” differ between these cases.

Second objection: If the eternal power and will eternally relate to bringing the world into existence, the world must be eternal, since a complete cause cannot be delayed from its effect. If the relation is originated, its origination requires a further relation, and so infinitely. Reply: An eternal will can intend from eternity that the world exist at a future time. A new relation of power or will need not be created by another relation: its occurrence can follow from the attribute itself. In addition, taʿalluqāt, relations of an attribute to its object, are intellectual considerations, and the alleged regress terminates when the consideration terminates.

Third objection: If every positive and negative condition necessary for the effect is present, the effect must follow and the agent cannot refrain; if some condition is absent, the effect cannot occur. There is thus supposedly no difference between an agent acting by choice and one necessitating by its essence. Reply: Even conceding that no effect can be absent when the free agent's total conditions are complete, this does not make him a necessitating cause in the disputed sense. Necessity consequent upon free choice confirms rather than abolishes choice. If he willed to refrain, he could refrain, unlike the intrinsically necessitating agent.

Fourth objection: Power must relate equally to the existence and nonexistence of its object. But original nonexistence is beginningless and cannot be an effect of a capable agent; it is mere negation, not something upon which power can work. Reply: Saying nonexistence lies within power means that, if the agent wills not to produce something, it does not produce it; or if it does not will its production, it does not produce it. The incoherent claim would be that it produces nonexistence as a positive effect. The argument concerns the nature of power in any agent, not God alone.

Fifth objection: If God's action is preferable for Himself to refraining, He acquires perfection through another; if it is not preferable, the action is frivolous. Neither suits the Necessary. Reply: An action can be preferable in itself or for another without improving its agent. Even if what does not benefit its agent is defined as frivolous, the further claim that every such action is impossible for God needs proof.

Sixth objection: Freedom would make the impossible possible, or allow the beginningless to be an effect of power. If the effect was impossible in eternity but later possible, impossibility has turned into possibility. If it was already possible in eternity, then by being attributed to a capable agent it seems possible for a beginningless thing to be an effect. Reply: Something can be possible in itself even when its occurrence in eternity under the description of an originated effect is impossible. One cannot infer that power can produce a beginningless effect from the intrinsic possibility of the essence of an effect at all times.

Seventh objection: God's eternal knowledge determines whether an effect will occur. If He knows it will occur, the occurrence is necessary; if He knows it will not, it is impossible. Neither necessaries nor impossibilities can be objects of power, since the capacity to do otherwise is lost. Reply: God knows that the effect will occur through His power. A necessity consequent upon such a free act does not destroy its being within power; it presupposes and confirms it.

The infinity and universality of divine power

Conclusion. Divine power is infinite. If this means it has no extended nature that could reach a physical boundary, or that it never ceases to exist, the claim is straightforward. If it means that there is no final limit of possibility beyond which it becomes unable to relate to another possible object, this follows because such failure would be incapacity and defect. Many divine effects may themselves endure without end, such as the bliss of Paradise, whose successive instances are endless in possibility. The ground of God's being capable is His essence; the ground of an object being capable of receiving power's operation is its possibility. Neither ground terminates at some further possible thing.

This last argument is invoked for the universality of power over all possible beings. An objection observes that being possible does not by itself show that an object meets all the conditions for the attachment of power or lacks all impediments. A suggested answer denies there are differences among possible things before existence sufficient to distinguish their conditions; the author regards this as weak. The stronger appeal is to revealed statements of the universality of divine power, such as “God is powerful over all things.”

Disagreements about universality

The source reviews schools said to restrict the objects of divine power. The Majūs are represented as attributing evil and noxious things to another agent, Ahriman, in order to avoid making one ultimate being both good and evil. Al-Naẓẓām and his adherents are said to hold that God cannot create ignorance, falsehood, injustice and other ugly acts: if able to create them He could perform them, but their performance would imply folly if their ugliness were known, or ignorance if it were not. Reply: That a thing is ugly in relation to God is denied. Even if conceded, the ability to do it is compatible with the impossibility of its occurrence because the relevant motives are absent or countervailing reasons present. ʿAbbād and his followers deny God's ability to do what He knows will not occur, since its occurrence would be impossible; another report extends this to what He knows will occur, since its occurrence is necessary. The reply reprises the distinction of conditioned necessity from intrinsic impossibility of being an object of power.

Al-Kaʿbī and his adherents deny that God can produce an act similar to one within a servant's power; otherwise the same movement caused by God and by a servant would have to be alike. Their argument appeals to the supposition that a servant's act must be obedience, folly or humility (or, in variant summaries, obedience, disobedience and folly), descriptions they deny of divine acts. The proposed exhaustive disjunction is rejected: acts can pursue ordinary worldly benefit without being obedience or humility, which specifically include submission or reverence to another. Moreover, the intrinsic object of power is a movement or rest; the moral or intentional descriptions attend it in virtue of the servant's aims and motives and do not constitute an essential difference in the movement itself.

Al-Jubbāʾī and his followers deny that God can produce the very same individual effect within a servant's power, lest one effect be created by two creators, because a complete motive and power would make it occur through each. Reply on the theologians' account: The servant's power is not, in the relevant sense, an independent producer. Even conceding some efficiency to it, the presence of one agent's power or will might prevent the completion of the other's conditions. And even if both co-operated, the effect could be attributed to their joint agency, rather than independently to each. Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī offers the example of a single body connected to two people, one pulling and another pushing, with the resulting motion attributed to both; the author remarks that this requires scrutiny.

A crucial threefold distinction of “universality” now follows. (1) God is capable of every possible thing, whether or not that thing is ever willed or produced by Him or whether some created power is said to produce it. The foregoing controversies primarily concern this sense. (2) Every actually existing possible thing depends on God directly or through intermediaries. Monotheists agreeing upon one Necessary Existent do not ordinarily contest this abstract dependency, although they dispute the mediators and precise dependency relations. (3) All beings other than God's essence and attributes exist immediately by His power and will, with no other efficient producer. This is the stronger account adopted by certain Sunni theologians, including Ashʿarīs; it must not be confused with the previous two.

Defenders of (3) adduce scriptural language that God alone is the Creator and in particular creates heaven and earth, darkness and light, death and life, substances and accidents. Their proof from concurrence of independent powers (tawārud) argues that if another power produces a thing which lies also within God's power, and the two wills simultaneously determine the one effect, then production by one rather than the other is an arbitrary preference without a preferent; production independently by both would make one effect depend on two separately sufficient causes. In the case of two persons pushing or pulling one body, however, neither individual is proved independently sufficient to produce that determinate motion. A possible rejoinder is that divine power is the stronger of the two, and the created power is thereby ineffective.

The proof from mutual hindrance (tamānuʿ) assumes God's will and an alleged independent creator's will simultaneously determine opposites, such as motion and rest of one body at one time. If both happen, opposites coexist; if neither happens, God's power is frustrated and the body lacks both motion and rest; if one happens, there is allegedly a preference without a preferent. An opponent may answer that divine power is more perfect. This need not mean merely that it operates on more kinds of objects, while its influence on this particular object is equal. It may mean greater efficacy in the very act, such that divine power prevails and the creature's supposed power fails.

Positions of philosophers and other groups

The claim that God alone is the immediate effective cause of every existence is characteristic of some Sunni theologians, while numerous other groups differ. The philosophers say the first immediate effect of the Necessary is a separate intellect, from which follow an intellect, a soul and a celestial sphere in successive orders. Intellects produce the spheres; souls produce their movements; terrestrial occurrences arise through their principles, substantial forms, powers, and the mediation of celestial movements. Particular forms explain the operations of minerals, and souls those of plants and animals. Many possible beings thus possess efficiency in their account.

The astral determinists and astrologers attribute sublunary changes to the states, positions, movements and conjunctions of the heavenly bodies. Their principal inference is from observed concomitant variation (dawarān) of phenomena with celestial states. This does not conclusively prove causality: the celestial conditions could be instruments, prerequisites or simultaneous results. Miracles and extraordinary occurrences are also offered against rigid predictions. The school additionally assumes heavenly simplicity and regularity while introducing sharply differing qualities and dominions of signs, degrees and planets. The naturalists likewise infer from correlations that terrestrial occurrences proceed through the mixtures, powers and qualities of elements. Al-Taftāzānī notes that these views may be classified under philosophy, but are separately attributed because their advocates' positions on the first principles—separate intellects, celestial souls, whether God chooses, and so on—may be unknown.

Among Muslims the Muʿtazilites attribute voluntary deeds to human and animal agents; the case is developed in the later discussion of the creation of acts. The source also groups with them certain explanations of evil acts by the devil, a polemical comparison requiring particular care in historical attribution.

Final terminological qualification. An objection asks why philosophers who deny God's action through free power are included among deniers of its universality rather than deniers of power altogether. Here “power” sometimes means simply being capable (qādiriyya). The philosophers can use an account on which a capable agent is one from whom an action could or could not issue, with will or its absence determining the issue and the action necessarily following when will is present. Their will is treated as a specific knowledge, and their knowledge and power are beginningless and not really additional to the essence. Under this formulation they nevertheless maintain an eternal world and a Maker necessitating through His essence. Al-Taftāzānī's judgment is that this preserves the words ‘power’ and ‘will’ but not the intended freedom they signify.

Textual and doctrinal cautions: Some terms and punctuation are introduced to make the dialectical progression readable. The six proofs, seven counterarguments, three senses of universality, and several school attributions should be checked against printed pages and any variant critical editions before publication. The model of free agency must not be reduced either to bare chance or to necessitating action independent of will.

### Demonstrations that the Maker knows

**“The third investigation is that He is knowing.”** The great majority of rational thinkers agree on this. Two arguments are commonly offered by the theologians.

**First**, God produces a work displaying **firmly ordered and accomplished craftsmanship**, and whoever produces such a work knows. The major premise is taken as evident: whoever sees beautifully fashioned writing or hears eloquent words conveying subtle meanings and sound purposes is certain that their producer has knowledge. The minor premise follows from God's being the maker of the spheres and elements, with their substances, accidents, kinds of minerals, plants and animals, ordered in arrangements and relations that overwhelm human understanding. Astronomy, anatomy, celestial and terrestrial natural inquiry, zoology and botany witness to these wonders, whose details cannot be exhaustively recorded. People possess little knowledge even of the sensible world, much less of the spiritual world and the philosopher's immaterial beings. The Qurʾānic signs of the heavens and earth, changing day and night, ships, life-giving rain, living creatures, winds and clouds are cited.

**Objection:** If “well ordered” means that every feature is flawless and the best imaginable means to every benefit, the world manifestly contains evils and injuries. If it means ordered in some respects only, unintelligent natural powers and animals also produce regular arrangements. Philosophers even attribute the elaborate formation of bodily organs to an unconscious **formative power** (*quwwa muṣawwira*). Why call the major premise self-evident? **Reply:** The argument concerns the admirable subtleties of workmanship, varied arrangements and correspondence to useful purposes **to a high degree**, not the claim that no defect whatever or better possible order exists. The judgement that abundant, repeated, ingenious workmanship indicates knowledge is evident, even if its self-evidence escapes some thinkers. Repetition and variety remove the worry that the evidence amounts merely to weak opinion.

**Second**, God is **capable and freely choosing**, as established in the preceding investigation. Choice and purposive agency are inconceivable without knowing the object chosen. **Objection:** Bees, spiders and many birds and animals construct remarkably ordered dwellings and arrange their livelihoods, though not usually classified as intellectual knowers. **Reply:** Even conceding that the animals themselves produce those effects, why deny them an appropriate **degree of knowledge**, created in them continuously or bestowed as an impulse at the relevant time? The more rigorous theologians prefer this second route from freedom and choice to the first route from craftsmanship. The latter faces the troublesome alternative that God might create a **different knowing, capable agent** which immediately produces the accomplished works. To answer that producing such an agent and its knowledge is itself a still more accomplished work, hence requires knowledge, presupposes that God produces by **purpose and choice**. The argument from workmanship thus returns to the argument from agency, which independently supports the conclusion.

Some appeal to revealed statements and communal agreement. But belief that messengers are truly commissioned and scriptures genuinely revealed appears already to require affirming the sender's knowledge and power, making the proof circular. One reply says that miracles establish a messenger's truth before any explicit reflection on the sender's knowledge; the author calls this evasive. For **divine speech**, however, the parallel route may have more force, as al-Rāzī acknowledges.

### Two philosophers' arguments

**First**, the Necessary is **immaterial**, and every immaterial being is an intellect or knows universals. The second premise is argued through an immaterial object's independence of material impediments: since nothing needs to be removed or altered in it before it can become intelligible, it is intelligible in itself. Possible intelligibility entails possible companionship (*muṣāḥaba*) between the intelligible and the intellect grasping it. That possibility cannot await the object's actually inhering in an intellect, for otherwise the possibility of companionship would depend on its actual occurrence. Whether the immaterial object exists in the mind or externally, it can thus accompany an intellect. If intellectual apprehension is this companionship, whatever the immaterial substance can intellectually apprehend must already be actual in it: only matter admits a transition from potency to act. Al-Taftāzānī criticises several steps of this reasoning as weak. If the companionship of an immaterial existent with intelligibles really sufficed for knowing them, the argument would already be complete without the rest.

**Second**, God knows **His own essence**. On the philosophical account, an immaterial being's intellectual presence to itself needs no second representative image; such an image would be a pointless duplication. Knowing its own essence is its being present to itself rather than hidden from itself. Even if this argument proves knowledge in general only by relying on disputed philosophical premises, the philosophers continue to knowledge of other things: God knows Himself as the **principle of possibles**, and knowing a principle or cause implies knowing its consequences and effects. **Objection:** Even an immediate consequence of an essence need not be an evident consequence which is automatically understood when the essence is conceived. Consider a triangle and the equality of its angles to two right angles. If every consequent were automatically known, then all remote consequences would also be known by perpetual inference. **Reply:** Here the premise concerns **complete knowledge of a thing as it is in itself**, not partial human apprehension; God's knowledge of Himself is complete.

### Objections denying knowledge and answers

Those who deny divine knowledge invoke two broad arguments.

**First**, knowledge of self or others would involve plurality. If knowledge is a **relation**, or a property with a relation, the knower and known must be two distinct terms; the absolutely one cannot know itself. Knowledge of other things introduces further multiplicity, since knowing one object differs from knowing another, and knowledge as a form representing its object would require innumerable different forms in the one divine essence. **Reply in respect of self-knowledge:** A distinction **according to consideration** can suffice, as it does when a person knows the very self that is knowing. An objection charges circularity: if considering the self as knower and known presupposes knowledge, how can that distinction be a condition of knowledge? But the condition need not be **temporally or causally prior**; the requirement may be that knowledge and the distinction are inseparable. The example does not presume that the human self consists of numerically different substances designated knower and known.

**Reply concerning other objects:** Divine knowledge need not be a multiplicity of representational forms **impressed in** the divine essence. It may be one power of knowledge with multiple **relations** to its objects. An alternative philosophical analysis says that effects are present to their cause by necessary production; a person's imagined image is produced with some contribution from an external object and is nevertheless apprehended *through itself* rather than through a second image that would multiply representations indefinitely. Much more can a self-sufficient cause apprehend what proceeds from it without needing imprinted forms. The condition of knowing is an object's being **present to** the knower, not necessarily inhering in it: self-knowledge itself illustrates that. Created effects are present to their necessary intellectual source without inhering in it. Al-Taftāzānī adds that, in any event, Sunni theologians do not accept as a universal principle the philosophers' prohibition of all real plurality of divine attributes.

**Second**, if knowledge differs from the divine essence, it is a possible entity requiring explanation. Yet God cannot receive His perfection from another. The same divine being would therefore be both **producer and receiver**, which is alleged impossible. **Reply:** Deny that one and the same being can never in any respect be an efficient source and a subject of an inseparable attribute. The universal impossibility has not been established.

### The infinity and total scope of knowledge

**Conclusion.** Divine knowledge is without limit: it does not cease, never becomes unable to relate to an object of knowledge, and extends to what is infinite, such as numbers, figures and the successive delights of Paradise. It includes **existing and nonexistent things, possibles and impossibles, universals and particulars**. Scriptural texts affirm that God knows every thing, that no tiny thing escapes Him, and that He knows what eyes conceal and hearts hide, openly declared and secret.

The rational argument appeals to the divine essence as the ground of knowing—whether through a distinct attribute of knowledge, as real-attribute theorists hold, or without that mediation—and to the possibility of being known as the ground in the object. Because God's essence stands in the same relation to all knowables, limitation to some would require an external specifier, incompatible with divine necessity and complete independence.

**Objection from recursive self-knowledge:** If God knows His knowledge, He knows that knowledge of knowledge, and so on without end; this produces infinitely many actually existing attributes, allegedly impossible. The source refuses the facile answer that knowledge simply **is** the divine essence, since that was contested earlier. But it denies that knowledge of knowledge must be a further external **attribute**: one knowledge can have multiple intellectual or relational *taʿalluqāt*. Even if a relation differs according to its object, that does not entail infinitely many distinct real attributes in the divine subject. The absence of an external relational entity does not mean that the real predication “God knows this” is false. Al-Rāzī alternatively proposes that these self-directed objects are infinite **without last member**, whereas a proof against an infinite past would have another scope; the more useful answer in this discussion is to distinguish a real attribute from the infinity of its relations.

**Objection concerning infinitely many knowables:** Every known thing must be distinguished; the infinite, as a whole, cannot be delimited and so cannot be distinguished. Moreover, infinitely many known objects appear to demand infinitely many distinct knowledges. **Replies:** Distinction from something other need not make the distinguished thing finite. Knowing an infinite multitude means knowing each of its members; each member may be distinguished, though the multitude is unbounded. An alternative suggestion distinguishes an entire collection from anything beyond it, but then there may be nothing beyond **all existents and nonexistents**. Such an external boundary is not a condition of knowing each item. The plurality of known objects still does not multiply the external divine knowledge itself. Against knowledge of **nonexistents**, the objection confuses physical individuation with intelligible distinction: what does not exist outside the mind can nevertheless have a determinable conceptual object.

### Philosophers and the knowledge of changing particulars

The received description of the philosophers' position says that God cannot know **changing particulars as changing particulars**, in a manner that would introduce alteration into His essence or attributes. He knows time-bound events through an eternally fixed knowledge of their complete order, times and determinations, not by acquiring successive beliefs that a particular event is **about to happen, is now happening, and has happened**. Thus, if celestial motions establish that a lunar eclipse falls at such a date, God knows the entire dated configuration and its occurrences without His knowledge shifting from “will be” to “is” to “was.” The temporal variations belong to our modes of apprehension rather than to His timeless knowledge. This is not the flat assertion that He is ignorant of all individual events.

Al-Rāzī presses a stricter interpretation of some philosophical principles. If either **change** or **determinate material configuration** prevents the divine intellect from directly knowing a particular, then not only generated and corrupted bodies and accidents but also celestial spheres, even if immutable in their substantial natures, would be excluded by their shapes. An immaterial, unchanging individual (God or a separate intellect), by contrast, could be known: the principles that establish God knows His own essence and the first intellect are concerned with individuals as well. Al-Taftāzānī notes that this argument, if correct, concerns the categories of individuals it reaches; it cannot automatically be universalised without a separate premise.

**Principal philosophical argument:** Suppose God knows today that Zayd **will enter** a house tomorrow. Once tomorrow arrives and Zayd enters, continuing to know “he will enter tomorrow” would fail to correspond to reality; replacing it with “he has entered” seems to involve one divine cognition ceasing and another coming into existence. Such change is impossible in what is beginningless. **Theologians' reply:** Knowing is either a relation or a property bearing relations. A relation to a changing object can change without the subject in which it is grounded changing. A beginningless being can be “before” a newly arising event, “together with” it when it arises, and “after” it when it ceases, without itself undergoing alteration. If knowledge is **nothing but** the relation, then a changing relational designation need not change the essence; if it is a real attribute with changing relations, even the attribute itself need not change.

Many Muʿtazilites and Sunnis attempt a stronger answer: the eternal knowledge that an event **will occur** and the knowledge that it **has occurred** are, they say, numerically **one knowledge**, not successive properties. A person who continuously knows an arrival will occur may later recognise the arrival through the same stable cognition, without acquiring a new attribute. They argue that one divine knowledge is like a mirror displaying varied objects, or like an unchanged person who becomes to Zayd “on his right” after earlier being “on his left” because Zayd changes his position. These comparisons are challenged if knowledge is defined as the changing *relation itself*, rather than an enduring property supporting relations.

**Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī's three objections:** (1) Someone who believed yesterday that Zayd would enter the city today might sit in a dark room and fail to realise **today has arrived**; he would not thereby know that Zayd has already entered. Knowing that he **has entered** is a third cognition formed from the earlier prediction **together with** knowledge that its date has passed. (2) The first cognition concerns an event still future, the second one already actual; their objects and the conditions of truth differ. A representation or relation corresponding to one need not be identical to one corresponding to the other. (3) Either cognition can exist without the other: one may predict the arrival and never know that it happened, or learn of an arrival without ever having predicted it. The author grants that the two cognitions differ, but maintains that **difference in a relation or knowing-state does not entail alteration of the divine essence**.

Another response maintains that **both temporally indexed relations are eternal and unchanged**. God eternally knows that Zayd does not enter on Friday and does enter on Saturday. What changes is the propriety, from our changing temporal standpoint, of the words “will enter,” “is entering” and “has entered,” not the eternally true, dated content. In the same fashion He knows eternally the world's nonexistence in an earlier interval, its existence later, and its subsequent passing. A philosopher's objection that a knowledge “the world is now nonexistent” would be contradicted when the world exists confuses the dated content “it did not exist **then**” with an assertion that it does not exist **now**. These are different propositions.

**Abū al-Ḥusayn's own view:** Divine knowledge of changing particulars does **change with their occurrence**, and this does not change God's essence. The source compares this to reports concerning Jahm b. Ṣafwān and Hishām b. al-Ḥakam. On this account God eternally knows essences and natures, but certain affirmative judgements—that a specific entity has arisen or passed away—and certain individual presentations arise under the conditions of their objects' occurrence. The immutable essence grounds knowing **subject to those originated conditions**. The changing *taʿalluqāt* or qualifying relations need not be originated substantial modifications; neither must an eternal source's effects be eternal if their existence presupposes originated conditions.

Al-Rāzī's attempted refutation is that an eternal essence either suffices to establish an attribute, in which case it eternally has it, or requires a separate condition, in which case the essence is dependent on that condition and therefore contingent.
