Demonstrations that the Maker knows

“The third investigation is that He is knowing.” The great majority of rational thinkers agree on this. Two arguments are commonly offered by the theologians.

First, God produces a work displaying firmly ordered and accomplished craftsmanship, and whoever produces such a work knows. The major premise is taken as evident: whoever sees beautifully fashioned writing or hears eloquent words conveying subtle meanings and sound purposes is certain that their producer has knowledge. The minor premise follows from God's being the maker of the spheres and elements, with their substances, accidents, kinds of minerals, plants and animals, ordered in arrangements and relations that overwhelm human understanding. Astronomy, anatomy, celestial and terrestrial natural inquiry, zoology and botany witness to these wonders, whose details cannot be exhaustively recorded. People possess little knowledge even of the sensible world, much less of the spiritual world and the philosopher's immaterial beings. The Qurʾānic signs of the heavens and earth, changing day and night, ships, life-giving rain, living creatures, winds and clouds are cited.

Objection: If “well ordered” means that every feature is flawless and the best imaginable means to every benefit, the world manifestly contains evils and injuries. If it means ordered in some respects only, unintelligent natural powers and animals also produce regular arrangements. Philosophers even attribute the elaborate formation of bodily organs to an unconscious formative power (quwwa muṣawwira). Why call the major premise self-evident? Reply: The argument concerns the admirable subtleties of workmanship, varied arrangements and correspondence to useful purposes to a high degree, not the claim that no defect whatever or better possible order exists. The judgement that abundant, repeated, ingenious workmanship indicates knowledge is evident, even if its self-evidence escapes some thinkers. Repetition and variety remove the worry that the evidence amounts merely to weak opinion.

Second, God is capable and freely choosing, as established in the preceding investigation. Choice and purposive agency are inconceivable without knowing the object chosen. Objection: Bees, spiders and many birds and animals construct remarkably ordered dwellings and arrange their livelihoods, though not usually classified as intellectual knowers. Reply: Even conceding that the animals themselves produce those effects, why deny them an appropriate degree of knowledge, created in them continuously or bestowed as an impulse at the relevant time? The more rigorous theologians prefer this second route from freedom and choice to the first route from craftsmanship. The latter faces the troublesome alternative that God might create a different knowing, capable agent which immediately produces the accomplished works. To answer that producing such an agent and its knowledge is itself a still more accomplished work, hence requires knowledge, presupposes that God produces by purpose and choice. The argument from workmanship thus returns to the argument from agency, which independently supports the conclusion.

Some appeal to revealed statements and communal agreement. One reply says that miracles establish a messenger's truth before any explicit reflection on the sender's knowledge; the author calls this evasive. For divine speech, however, the parallel route may have more force, as al-Rāzī acknowledges.

First, the Necessary is immaterial, and every immaterial being is an intellect or knows universals. Those who deny divine knowledge invoke two broad arguments.

If knowledge is a relation, or a property with a relation, the knower and known must be two distinct terms; the absolutely one cannot know itself. title: Divine will (*irāda*): specification, rival definitions and what God wills

**Source:** digital II.93–96, source characters 1129512–1137902 (exclusive). **Status:** new source-ordered explanatory English rendering, requiring printed-edition comparison.

**“The fourth investigation.”** The theologians, philosophers and other schools generally agree that God is **willing** (*murīd*), a description frequent in the Qurʾān and prophetic speech. God's being an agent **by choice** implies intention and will. “Choosing” highlights the consideration of **both alternatives** and a preference for one; “willing” highlights the alternative actually preferred. The controversy concerns the **nature of that will**.

According to the author's school, will is an **eternal real attribute**, additional to the essence and subsisting in it. The **Jubbāʾites** regard will as an additional attribute subsisting **without a locus**. The **Karrāmiyya** make it an originated attribute inhering in the essence. **Dirār** identifies it with the essence. **Al-Najjār** explains it negatively, as the agent's not being coerced or inattentive. The **philosophers** identify it with God's knowledge of the **best possible order**. **Al-Kaʿbī** identifies God's will of His own action with His knowing it, and His will of another's action with His commanding it. Some leading Muʿtazilites identify will with knowledge of the benefit in an action.

The proof offered by the attribute-theorists is that among equally possible opposites **one** occurs and not the other, and at **one time** rather than another. God's essence relates equally to the alternatives; a **specifying attribute** is needed, because determination without a determiner is impossible, and the Necessary cannot depend in His agency on an external source. That attribute is **will**: the evident notion of a preference or determination of one of the power's two possible objects, performing and refraining. It differs from **power**, which relates equally to the alternatives, and from **knowledge**, which as knowledge of alternatives does not itself determine one. An argument that knowledge of a future act precedes the will while knowledge of an accomplished act follows the event is open to objection; in the relevant sense, knowledge **follows the known** because it represents what the known thing is, not because its existence must be later in time. The stronger contention is that will as the **source of specification** is distinct from knowledge and power, with its eternity and real status defended by arguments comparable to those for the other attributes.

**First objection:** Will, too, is equally capable of attaching to either act and every possible time. If it intrinsically preferred one alternative, the other would cease to be possible and free choice would disappear. If it did not, its determination would demand another specifying cause, and an infinite regress of wills would result. **Reply:** Will's very **nature** is to specify, including between equal alternatives and even where one appears less attractive. This does not mean a possible being exists **without a producer**. Nor does the effect becoming necessary through a **chosen willing** remove freedom: necessity **through choice** is the accomplishment of choice, not its abolition.

**Second objection:** Will must cease when what was willed is accomplished; an eternal attribute would therefore perish. Or an eternal will would entail an eternal effect and hence the world's eternity. **Reply:** The attribute remains, while its **relation** to a particular event under a particular condition may cease. Moreover, an eternal will can determine from eternity that the world be brought about at its appointed **originated time**. Time presents a further problem when it is itself to be originated; one possibility is to treat the specifying temporal determination as a mental or estimative consideration rather than a self-subsisting prior time. The distinction between will and **its relation** to an effect also answers the claim that a will without a present object is impossible. The effect is contingent in relation to the attribute considered by itself, but determinate once that attribute's relation to the effect is specified.

**Third objection:** If God's willing something makes it better **for Him** to act, He is perfected by something other than Himself; otherwise acting would be useless. The answer is the same as in the investigation on power: an act may be appropriate or beneficial in itself or for another without improving God, and the alleged universal prohibition of action without benefit to God needs proof.

Among contrary schools, the **Karrāmiyya's originated will** is rejected because originated realities cannot, on the author's principles, inhere in God's essence; moreover a new divine act would require a will, making an originated will depend upon another will, and so circularly or indefinitely. A counterproposal says that divine attributes may necessarily follow from the essence when an originated condition is present. The response invokes the denied infinity of successive originated prerequisites; if the prerequisites are divine qualities, originated qualities would follow, whereas if they are external, divine perfection would depend on something outside God.

The majority of **Basran Muʿtazilites** are said to posit an originated will subsisting **in no subject**. The author objects that a self-subsisting thing is not properly an **attribute**. It is insufficient merely to insist that an accident always needs a subject when the theologians also deny that God's attributes are accidents; the difficulty is the incompatible predications “subsists by itself” and “is an attribute of another.”

The **philosophers' providence** (*ʿināya*) consists in the eternal intellectual presentation of the entire best-ordered series of existents and their appointed times. This knowledge is said to necessitate the emanation of just that order. Their denial of a further free intention is thus part of the doctrine itself: they cannot be credited with admitting the theologians' real attribute of choice simply because they employ the term **will**. Al-Najjār's negative account and al-Kaʿbī's accounts in terms of knowledge or command are similarly criticised for insufficiently expressing the **determination of one thing rather than another at its particular time**. Command is especially distinct from will: the source insists that God can command a servant to do something that He does not will to occur.

**Will versus motive.** Several Muʿtazilites identify willing with the prevailing **motive** (*dāʿī*): knowledge, belief or opinion that an act or refraining contains benefit. Because opinion and mere belief are not attributed to God, they identify divine will with **knowledge of benefit**. They argue that willing is the **agent's act**, as shown by praise, blame, reward and punishment for intentions; if it were an act in addition to a motive, the agent would have to be aware of this additional decision, but introspection finds no preferent beyond the prevailing motive. **Reply:** To say “a person wills” no more proves that the will is his voluntary production than “he is capable” or “he is unable” proves that his power or incapacity is itself intentionally produced. If will were another voluntary act, it would need a **prior will**, creating a regress. Praise and blame may concern the consequences of a will, the intentional acquisition of motives or the removal of impediments. More fundamentally, introspection does disclose a **tendency or inclination** distinct from the cognition of advantage; it may arise from the motive or arise without it and serve as the **proximate basis of choice**. A thirsty person selecting one of two equivalent cups, or a fugitive one of two equivalent paths, can make a selection without judging one more beneficial than the other. Therefore will is not identical with merely perceiving some benefit. One might separately deny this kind of **inclination** of God and make His knowledge of benefit sufficient; that is a different thesis requiring its own proof.

**Conclusion:** According to the people of truth, **whatever God wills occurs**, and **everything that occurs is willed by Him**, although some things are neither **pleasing** to Him nor **commanded** by Him and may indeed be forbidden. The formula attributed to the early authorities is that what God wills comes to be, and what He does not will does not come to be. The Muʿtazilites disagree on both principles, arguing that God wishes faith and obedience from unbelievers and sinners although it does not occur, whereas their disbelief and sins occur although God does not will them. The more detailed debate is explicitly **postponed to the discussion of acts and the creation of human deeds**; this investigation should not be made to resolve that debate prematurely.

**Editorial caution:** The claims about the Karrāmiyya, Muʿtazila, philosophers and other named groups are *reports in the source*, some polemical. The distinction between free **choice**, will as **eternal attribute**, and its **temporally specified relation** must be kept intact.

Editorial caution: The claims about the Karrāmiyya, Muʿtazila, philosophers and other named groups are reports in the source, some polemical. The distinction between free choice, will as eternal attribute, and its temporally specified relation must be kept intact.

title: Life, hearing, sight, and other modes of cognition
en:
**Source:** electronic vol. II, pp. 96–98, canonical source characters 1137902–1142206 (exclusive). **Status:** new close explanatory working rendering, scan and clause checking outstanding.

**“The fifth investigation.”** That the Maker is **living, hearing and seeing** (*ḥayy, samīʿ, baṣīr*) is known necessarily from the religion and established in the Qurʾān and Sunna, such that it cannot be denied or reinterpreted away. The source reports agreement among the adherents of the religious communities and rational thinkers. In addition to transmission, arguments are offered. God is **knowing and powerful**, and whatever possesses knowledge and power is living. Hearing and vision are among the perfections to which a living being is susceptible; whatever perfection is possible for the Necessary exists in Him actually, since He is not potentially endowed with a perfection that still awaits actualisation. More generally, to lack an actual perfection one is capable of having would be a deficiency, and the Necessary is free of deficiency.

This form of argument does not require one first to establish that death, deafness and blindness are **positive contraries** to life, hearing and sight rather than **privations**, or that a being must possess either a perfection or a contrary. It does, however, require a bridge from **living beings among us** to the Necessary Existent: why should life in the unseen divine case make hearing and sight appropriate? Al-Juwaynī's procedure of **exhaustive examination and division** (*sabr wa-taqsīm*) begins with the observation that an inanimate object does not receive hearing or sight; when it becomes living, and no disabling condition intervenes, it does. Examining its other features, one finds life the relevant condition for receptivity. The same condition is then applied to the divine case. Al-Ghazālī offers a more direct argument from **perfection**: a living, hearing and seeing creature is more perfect in the relevant respect than one who lacks these perfections. It is absurd to make human beings or animals more perfect than their Maker. Walking and beauty of face are not counterexamples, because those bodily properties are known to be inapplicable to the Necessary, unlike the cognitive perfections under discussion.

Why so many proofs when revelation is already decisive? People differ in what moves them to conviction; some attain assurance from one argument, others from several converging arguments. Every proof may invite technical objection, while a combination can yield stronger conviction. Moreover, denial of divine defects need not be based exclusively on consensus and scriptural authority. A thinker may recognise it independently, or not concede the authority of consensus, or judge that relying upon revelation would presuppose the very knowledge and power of God that enable the sending of prophets.

Given life, hearing and sight, the author's school affirms **eternal attributes** of life, hearing and vision, according to its earlier defence of divine knowledge and power. **Objection:** If hearing and vision are eternal, the audible and visible objects must also be eternal: there can be no hearing without something heard. **Reply:** An eternal attribute may have **originated relations** to its objects, just as knowledge and power do. The opponent may insist that the attributes must be either originated—making God a locus of originated qualities—or eternal—making audible and visible things eternal. The distinction of enduring attribute from its relations answers both horns.

Another objection argues that being living, hearing and seeing entails being a **body**. Life is described by natural philosophers as a species-specific balance of a living mixture or as a power accompanying sensation and voluntary movement; hearing and sight are bodily organs' modifications by sensible things, or cognitive states that follow those modifications. **Reply:** Even in creatures, such bodily conditions are only **concomitants** of living and perceiving, not established as the essence of life or vision. Their presence alongside life in the observable world does not warrant requiring bodily structure in the unseen divine case.

The Ashʿarite school commonly treats hearing and sight as attributes **distinct from knowledge**. Yet on a report of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī's account of sensation, perceiving a sensible thing is a kind of **knowing that thing**. It is therefore not an unavoidable consequence of that account that hearing and sight are two distinct attributes in addition to divine knowledge. Hearing might be knowledge of audible things and sight knowledge of visible things. **Objection:** Knowledge of differing kinds of object is not necessarily one species of knowledge. **Reply:** One real attribute of knowledge might have different **relations** or modes of apprehension, such as an intellectual understanding of a visible thing and the visual apprehension of it. Philosophers and certain Baghdad Muʿtazilites deny additional real attributes altogether, while other Muʿtazilites distinguish being hearing or seeing from being knowing without accepting attributes really additional to the essence.

**Final question from al-Juwaynī:** If God possesses all appropriate cognitive perfections, should He be described by the **judgements** attaching to perception of tastes, odours, warmth, cold, softness and roughness? He argues affirmatively for the perfection of perception, but refuses bodily verbs such as **smelling, tasting and touching** of God: these suggest physical contact, whereas one can touch or smell an object and still fail to apprehend the relevant quality. The perfection in question is **cognitive disclosure**, not contact with an organ.

**Editorial note:** The distinction between the **cognitive reality** of hearing and vision and the bodily physiological conditions accompanying human sensation is central. References to a claim as al-Ashʿarī's, al-Juwaynī's or al-Ghazālī's should be checked in their own texts before treating it as a historically verified quotation.

title: MQ-C05-014 — Sixth investigation: the divine attribute of speech (*kalām*)
en:
# MQ-C05-014 — Sixth investigation: the divine attribute of speech (*kalām*)

**Arabic source:** source characters 1142206–1160086 (exclusive); printed volume II, pp.98–105. **Status:** continuous source-ordered first-pass explanatory translation, without independent page-image or clause verification. Objections are attributed to their reported proponents rather than silently made the author's conclusions.

### The affirmation of divine speech and the disagreement concerning its nature

The prophets have repeatedly affirmed that God **speaks**, and their truthfulness is established by the indication of miracles without depending upon God's verbal report that they are truthful; otherwise the proof would involve a circle. A rational demonstration is also attempted by analogy with hearing and sight: for a being capable of speech—namely one who lives, knows and has power—lack of speech is a defect, or possession of what is contrary to it, and defect is impossible in God. Even if someone disputes whether silence necessarily constitutes a defect, especially when the silent person has the power of speech, there remains the judgement that one who can speak is more perfect in that respect than one who cannot, and a creature cannot surpass the Creator in perfection. Here the objections and replies parallel those already advanced concerning hearing and sight.

There is thus no disagreement among adherents of religions and theological schools about applying **speaker** (*mutakallim*) to the Creator. The disagreement concerns **what His speech is** and whether it is beginningless or originated. According to the people of truth, His speech is not of the same genus as voices and letters; it is an **eternal attribute subsisting in the divine essence**, opposed to silence and to an impediment to speech such as muteness or infant incapacity. By this attribute He commands, forbids, informs and does the rest. Spoken expression, writing and signs indicate it. When expressed in Arabic it is the Qurʾān, in Greek the Gospel, in Hebrew the Torah, and in Syriac the Psalter: the formulations differ, not the underlying signified speech—just as one God may be mentioned in many languages.

The other schools reject this account, maintaining that speech is nothing but **ordered, audible letters signifying intended meanings**, and that a *speech subsisting in the soul* (*kalām nafsī*) has no intelligible reality. Their positions, however, differ sharply. Those Hanbalites and literalists whom the author here polemically calls *ḥashwiyya* suppose that these successive sounds and letters, notwithstanding the ordering in which a later letter of a word comes after an earlier, have existed eternally in God's essence. They hold that what is heard from reciters and seen in written Qurʾāns is the selfsame ancient speech. Reports that some even declared the manuscript's leather cover eternal or believed that the physical thing on which letters were written became eternal after having originated are adduced by the author as evidence of the absurdity he attributes to this view. These claims are **reported polemically**, not established descriptions of every member of the named school.

The **Karrāmiyya** avoid making temporally successive sounds eternal. They allow originated audible speech to subsist in God's essence. They distinguish His eternal *speech*, which they identify with His **power to speak**, from His originated *saying*. Something which starts and subsists in His essence is *originated* (*ḥādith*) by His power but, in their usage, not *brought into being* (*muḥdath*); what is separate from His essence is brought into being through the word **Be!**, not through power. The distinction is explained within their own technical terminology. The **Muʿtazila** hold that the articulated letters are originated but deny that anything originated subsists in the divine essence. To call God a speaker consequently means that He **creates speech in some body**. Some avoid calling the Qurʾān *created* because common speech could associate that designation with fabrication, while the greater number accept the term.

Among Muʿtazilites, the preference of **Abū Hāshim and later followers** is that speech consists of successive voices and letters, so that a written set of letters on the Preserved Tablet or in a codex is not itself the Qurʾān in that immediate audible sense; the Qurʾān is the recitation made by the reciter, an ordered succession of sounds created by God. **Al-Jubbāʾī**, in the report given here, maintains that speech belongs to a genus other than mere letters; it is heard upon hearing sounds, occurs through arrangements of letters and writing, continues with what is written and remembered, and is present in the Preserved Tablet, every codex and every tongue. Nonetheless it remains numerically one despite the multiplication or destruction of codices. These are distinct accounts even within the broadly created-speech position.

Two familiar syllogisms are therefore set against one another. One yields the **eternity of God's speech**: it is an attribute of God, and His attributes are eternal. The other yields its **origination**: speech is a species of sound, and sounds originate. Both cannot be true in an unqualified sense of the same entity, so each party rejects a premise. Muʿtazilites deny that speech is an attribute subsisting in God; Karrāmiyya deny that every divine attribute is eternal; Ashʿarites deny that speech, properly so called, consists of sounds and letters; those designated *ḥashwiyya* deny that the articulated sequence must originate. Setting aside the author's criticisms of the latter two alternatives, the principal dispute between Ashʿarites and Muʿtazilites becomes the **existence of internal speech** and whether the Qurʾān names that internal speech or the ordered audible utterance. Both agree that the sensory utterance originates; if eternal internal speech were established, the Muʿtazila would not contest its eternity as an eternal divine attribute simply on that supposition. The report of Abū Ḥanīfa and Abū Yūsuf disputing for six months before judging the attribution “created” to the Qurʾān unbelief must, according to the author, be understood with this precise point of dispute in view.

### First argument: a speaker is one in whom speech subsists

**Our first proof** is that the one properly called a *speaker* is the one **in whom speech subsists**, not merely someone who produces speech in another receptacle. The cause of movement in another body is not thereby called *moving*, nor is God called *voiced* simply because He creates sounds. Hearing someone utter “I am standing,” we call that person a speaker even if we do not know that he created the sound—and even if, following our doctrine, we know that God is the creator of the sound. Speech belonging to God must therefore subsist in Him; yet the sensory sequence of audible letters cannot subsist eternally in Him. It has a beginning and end, and one letter must be preceded by, and often conditioned on the ending of, the previous letter. Its parts do not exist simultaneously or endure after their utterance, as the earlier treatment of **quantity** explained. An originated accident cannot subsist in the divine essence. Hence the subsisting divine speech must be the **meaning**, since no third candidate for speech is available, and it must be eternal.

A **Muʿtazilite objection** holds that if speaking required a persisting accident in the subject, even human beings would not literally be called speakers: speech continually perishes and its sounds are located in the tongue rather than the whole person. Expressions such as “the prince speaks by the minister's tongue” and “the jinn speaks through the possessed person's tongue” also appear to separate speaker from substrate. A **literalist objection** says that the sequence of letters need not itself be successive: words are stored together in memory or impressed upon paper, and temporal order arises only when the bodily instrument of utterance produces them. The Qurʾān, encompassing order and meaning, could therefore be beginningless in God, even if the reading occurs in temporal order.

**Reply:** ordinary linguistic usage confirms that the speaker is the possessor of speech, and audible articulate sounds are necessarily successive and non-enduring. A transient accident may give a true name to its subject even without persisting, as with *moving* and *speaking*. Nor must an accident in every part of a bodily person inhere throughout the entire body for the person to be described by it; hearing, seeing and tasting operate through appropriate bodily parts. “Speaking through another's tongue” is figurative, signifying that the speaker supplies the words to another. The second objection changes the subject: the dispute concerns **audible letters**, not mental, remembered, depicted or written **representations** of them. Even an isolated, nonsuccessive sound is not a conceivable eternal attribute inhering in God's essence in the manner alleged.

### Second argument: an internal discourse distinct from knowledge and volition

A person uttering a command, prohibition, call, assertion, question or other speech act finds something **within the mind** which is expressed in these forms. That which is mentally entertained does not vary simply because the outward expressions differ by the conventions of languages. The speaker intends it to occur in the hearer's understanding so that the hearer may act or respond accordingly. This is what we call **speech of the soul** or inward discourse. Abū Hāshim is said to acknowledge something like it under the designation *thoughts* (*khawāṭir*).

That this inward discourse differs from **knowledge** and **will** is especially evident in assertion and in expressive utterances that are not requests. One may mistakenly identify **inward request** with volition and regard “I want you to do this but do not request it inwardly,” or its converse, as contradictory. The discussion will return to this matter in the chapter on divine acts. For the moment, an assertion can concern what a person does not know, even what he knows to be false, which distinguishes the content of assertion from his knowledge. Likewise a master can command a slave to perform something without willing that it be performed, for instance to establish the slave's disobedience and furnish an excuse for punishment. This is offered as a distinction between **command or request** and volition.

Al-Mawāqif suggests that Muʿtazilites might explain these cases as a will to undertake an action which **causes the hearer to believe** that the speaker knows what he asserts, or wills what he commands. The present author observes that he has not found exactly this explanation in their texts, but he has found something resembling it in the Muʿtazilite al-Zāhidī, who calls these cases displays of the **signs** of asserting or requesting, rather than genuine informing and requesting. Imām al-Ḥaramayn also anticipates a similar reply in the *Irshād*: perhaps what one finds inwardly is only a will to cause an uttered expression to be a command of obligation or recommendation. The answer is that the utterance has already passed while the request remains; the bygone expression itself is not presently willed, but perhaps regretted or missed. The internal state continuing after the utterance is not merely regret. Furthermore the utterance clearly **translates what is inwardly intended**, namely requirement or imposition, not merely a wish to attach a specific grammatical force to the utterance.

Ordinary Arabic similarly applies “speech” or “saying” to what exists inwardly: “There is speech within me”; “I fashioned a saying in my mind.” The reported verse of al-Akhṭal locates speech in the heart and makes the tongue its indication, and revelation speaks of what people **say within themselves**. If God is genuinely a speaker, while sensory sounds cannot subsist in His essence, then speech subsisting in Him is this internal non-sensory reality and is eternal.

### Objections concerning the Qurʾān and its revealed form

**First and second Muʿtazilite objections:** the Qurʾān is manifestly the ordered utterance of audible letters, a fact known in ordinary religious life even to the young, beginning with its praise of God and ending with the formula of seeking refuge; transmitted consensus identifies it in this way. Moreover its familiar properties known from text and consensus attach to the **temporally originated arrangement**, not to an internal eternal meaning. The response does not dispute that the name Qurʾān or *speech of God* is applied, through established linguistic usage or a well-known extension, to the sensory articulated form. This is the Quran commonly discussed by reciters, jurists and scholars of legal principles, and its letter-related properties are indeed originated.

The cited properties are these: the Qurʾān is **remembrance** (*dhikr*), and revelation describes newly arriving remembrance; it is **Arabic**, while the same meaning can be expressed in multiple languages, so being Arabic refers to its wording; it was **sent down** to the Prophet, while an eternal attribute subsisting in God's essence cannot literally move downward. An originated word, although an accident, can travel with the body or medium bearing it. The reports that the Qurʾān was first sent as a whole to the lower heaven, preserved or written there, and then conveyed gradually by Gabriel, are understood in this context. If someone argues that a manuscript contains only **written shapes** rather than sounds or concepts, one answers that writing signifies and represents words by the shapes of their letters. This distinction between represented word and the physical ink marks will matter below.

**A third objection:** the Qurʾān is the standing **challenge** (*taḥaddī*) to the Arabs to produce its equal. The challenge does not pertain to an eternal non-sensory attribute which remains perpetually beyond any specific occasion. **Reply:** the challenge is an event in which the Arabs are called to oppose the present articulated form by producing a comparable utterance; it is not a challenge to duplicate an eternal attribute. **A fourth objection:** the Qurʾān is subject to **abrogation**. Though a meaning as well as wording can be superseded, an eternal attribute cannot cease to exist; the kind of abrogation in question attaches to an originated wording or temporally applicable ruling.

**A further proof from the divine 'Be!'** is that the scriptural formula “Our word to something, when We will it, is only that We say to it 'Be!'” suggests a saying after willing to produce the thing and therefore an originated utterance. If one takes the word **thing** in the scope of the negation universally, however, an objection argues that even the saying “Be!” would need another preceding “Be!”, generating regress unless the saying is eternal. If the formula is merely figurative for immediate production, it loses force as evidence for an originated articulated speech. The reply examines the logic of the sentence: “Our saying to a thing when we bring it about is only this saying” restricts **what is said when saying takes place**; it does not entail that the saying is addressed to **every** thing, or that every saying is itself produced by a prior token of the same saying. Thus the asserted regress is not required by the wording.

### In what sense do reciters and manuscripts bear God's speech?

A common account among our school identifies the articulated Qurʾān as God's speech simply because it **indicates** His eternal speech, so that the identity of the person inventing the letters would be irrelevant. The present author prefers to add another special connection to God: revelation describes God as the **first producer** of the recorded shapes in the Preserved Tablet, or of the sounds in the tongue of the angel, or of a verbal disclosure to the Prophet. The descent upon the Prophet's heart, in the cited verse, strictly concerns **meaning** rather than transported ink or sound.

Some therefore make the name Qurʾān denote the **first individual ordered utterance** whose existence God originated. Later individual readings acquired by human reciters are *likenesses* of that first utterance, not numerically it. The preferable account takes the name to denote the articulated form **without specifying its first individual substrate**; the Qurʾān is one *by type*, so that what each reader recites is the Qurʾān itself, not merely something called its likeness. The same difference arises for a poem or a book attributed to its author. On either account, the name can denote the **complete text** alone, or a common expression applying to the whole and to each portion; the question is treated further in the commentary on *al-Tanqīḥ*.

Accordingly, several statements receive different interpretations. “What is written in every codex and recited on every tongue is God's speech” concerns **specific unity of form or type**. “What is read is a narration or likeness of God's speech, and His speech proper is what was first produced in the angel's tongue” concerns **individual identity**. “God's speech is not in a tongue or heart and does not inhabit a codex or tablet” concerns the **true eternal divine attribute**. The use of “God's speech *inhabits* a codex or tongue” was discouraged even when referring to the originated wording, both out of reverence and because it easily misleads hearers into imagining that the eternal attribute itself inheres in the created substrate.

Another answer makes the predications “Arabic,” “revealed,” “recited,” “heard,” and “written” apply figuratively to the **ancient meaning** because they literally apply to the sounds and letters which **indicate** it. One similarly says “I heard that meaning from him,” “I read it in a book,” or “I wrote it with my hand,” while what was materially heard, read or written was its verbal and graphic representation. On this approach, **recitation**—the reader's acquired sounds—is originated, and writing—the writer's movement and the visible letter figures—is originated. What is *recited*, *written*, *remembered in hearts*, and *heard* can be called eternal insofar as it means what is **understood through** those sounds and markings, not an entity literally inhering in a tongue, heart, or codex. Likewise *revelation* can signify that Gabriel apprehends God's speech in his proper station, descends, and makes the Prophet understand what he had apprehended, without the eternal speech being displaced from God's essence.

### Why is Moses singled out as the one spoken to by God?

If every believer may hear the originated Qurʾān and its eternal meaning can be understood through hearing, what marks Moses out as **Kalīm Allāh**? Several explanations are offered.

**First**, the view favored by al-Ghazālī, Moses heard **the eternal speech without sound or letters**, just as the divine essence may be seen in the Hereafter without bodily quantity or mode. This requires an account under which hearing, like vision, can be related to an existent other than sound, such an extraordinary relation being miraculous. **Second**, Moses heard a voice from **all directions**, contrary to ordinary hearing. **Third**, he heard it from a determinate direction, but in a sound that was **not acquired by a created human agent**: God Himself specially produced the voice and thus honored Moses with direct intelligible address. This last explanation is attributed to Abū Manṣūr al-Māturīdī and Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāyīnī. The latter reports that people agree that what is literally heard must be sound; some maintain that only sound is heard, while others apply *heard* to an inward meaning **known through** hearing sound, in which case the disagreement may be linguistic rather than substantive.

### Objection: eternal speech would contain false past-tense reports

**The third argument against eternal speech** reasons that revelation repeatedly says “We sent,” “Moses said,” “Pharaoh disobeyed,” and the like. The truth of a past-tense assertion requires the reported relation to have **already obtained**. No event can be earlier than eternity. If these assertions were all literally eternal past-tense reports, they would have been false when eternity had not yet been succeeded by the relevant events, and divine falsehood is impossible.

Several grounds for denying divine falsehood are listed: scholarly consensus; the certain prophetic reports whose authenticity is established by miracles without depending on God's speaking; the judgment of reason that lying is a defect involving signs of ignorance, incapacity or vain activity; and the impossibility that a beginningless falsehood should subsequently become a truth, since what is beginningless cannot change into its contrary, although a knower of the relation can certainly state the relation as it actually holds. The created Qurʾānic wording is interpreted as an expression of the eternal speech so that truth and falsehood ultimately concern the signified content.

Yet there is a further doctrinal difficulty. Some Ashʿarites deny that one can argue divine truthfulness simply from **lying's intrinsic badness**, since they do not grant the Muʿtazilite doctrine of rational moral ugliness. Imām al-Ḥaramayn and the author of *al-Talkhīṣ* maintain that appealing to its badness either accepts an independently rational ethical value or makes an argument from revelation which presupposes the divine truthfulness it is meant to establish. The author of *al-Mawāqif* sees no clear difference between calling lying a **defect** in reason and judging it intrinsically ugly, and the present author voices surprise at these theologians' way of stating the issue. An argument from miracles as a **special divine certification** may, in his view, break the supposed circle; but this is not a question to suppress by terminology.

**Principal answer:** eternal speech is not in itself characterized as **past, present or future**, because it does not occur in time. Those temporal descriptions arise later, through its **relations to temporal things** when their events and occasions obtain. The author nevertheless adds a striking qualification: explaining exactly how the eternal meaning is denoted by successive temporal wording is **extremely difficult**. So is an alternative that ascribes past, present and future entirely to the originated words while denying them to the eternal content. Both formulations require further thought.

### Objection: commands, prohibitions and reports without addressees

**The fourth argument** observes that God's speech includes command, prohibition, report, question and summons. If all such addresses were eternal in the way they address actual hearers, there would have been a command without anyone commanded, a prohibition without anyone prohibited, news without anyone listening, and a summons or question without a person addressed. This appears absurd and without wise purpose.

Five replies are reported. **(1)** ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān says that eternal speech as such is not yet any one of these types; it becomes command, prohibition and report later. The objection says that a genus cannot actually exist without being one of its species, and that change in the eternal is impossible. The reply invokes **one eternal attribute** appearing under diverse temporal relations without itself changing. **(2)** An actual addressee is required of sensory speech, but an inward address can suffice with the addressee's **intelligible existence**. **(3)** Futurity may be part of the command's object: commanding someone who is not yet born to obey **when he exists** does not mean absurdly commanding the nonexistent to act while nonexistent. A father anticipating his unborn son may make such a request; likewise the Prophet's commandments can reach believers born to the Day of Judgment. To confine his original addresses to his contemporaries and make every later application merely an analogy is implausible. Another formulation says the present are directly addressed, while the absent and unborn are comprehended **implicitly and subordinately**. The affirmation of divine speech and the disagreement concerning its nature

The prophets have repeatedly affirmed that God speaks, and their truthfulness is established by the indication of miracles without depending upon God's verbal report that they are truthful; otherwise the proof would involve a circle. A rational demonstration is also attempted by analogy with hearing and sight: for a being capable of speech—namely one who lives, knows and has power—lack of speech is a defect, or possession of what is contrary to it, and defect is impossible in God. Even if someone disputes whether silence necessarily constitutes a defect, especially when the silent person has the power of speech, there remains the judgement that one who can speak is more perfect in that respect than one who cannot, and a creature cannot surpass the Creator in perfection. Here the objections and replies parallel those already advanced concerning hearing and sight.

There is thus no disagreement among adherents of religions and theological schools about applying speaker (mutakallim) to the Creator. The disagreement concerns what His speech is and whether it is beginningless or originated. According to the people of truth, His speech is not of the same genus as voices and letters; it is an eternal attribute subsisting in the divine essence, opposed to silence and to an impediment to speech such as muteness or infant incapacity. By this attribute He commands, forbids, informs and does the rest. Spoken expression, writing and signs indicate it. When expressed in Arabic it is the Qurʾān, in Greek the Gospel, in Hebrew the Torah, and in Syriac the Psalter: the formulations differ, not the underlying signified speech—just as one God may be mentioned in many languages.

The other schools reject this account, maintaining that speech is nothing but ordered, audible letters signifying intended meanings, and that a speech subsisting in the soul (kalām nafsī) has no intelligible reality. Their positions, however, differ sharply. Those Hanbalites and literalists whom the author here polemically calls ḥashwiyya suppose that these successive sounds and letters, notwithstanding the ordering in which a later letter of a word comes after an earlier, have existed eternally in God's essence. They hold that what is heard from reciters and seen in written Qurʾāns is the selfsame ancient speech. Reports that some even declared the manuscript's leather cover eternal or believed that the physical thing on which letters were written became eternal after having originated are adduced by the author as evidence of the absurdity he attributes to this view. These claims are reported polemically, not established descriptions of every member of the named school.

The Karrāmiyya avoid making temporally successive sounds eternal. They allow originated audible speech to subsist in God's essence. They distinguish His eternal speech, which they identify with His power to speak, from His originated saying. Something which starts and subsists in His essence is originated (ḥādith) by His power but, in their usage, not brought into being (muḥdath); what is separate from His essence is brought into being through the word Be!, not through power. The distinction is explained within their own technical terminology. The Muʿtazila hold that the articulated letters are originated but deny that anything originated subsists in the divine essence. To call God a speaker consequently means that He creates speech in some body. Some avoid calling the Qurʾān created because common speech could associate that designation with fabrication, while the greater number accept the term.

Among Muʿtazilites, the preference of Abū Hāshim and later followers is that speech consists of successive voices and letters, so that a written set of letters on the Preserved Tablet or in a codex is not itself the Qurʾān in that immediate audible sense; the Qurʾān is the recitation made by the reciter, an ordered succession of sounds created by God. Al-Jubbāʾī, in the report given here, maintains that speech belongs to a genus other than mere letters; it is heard upon hearing sounds, occurs through arrangements of letters and writing, continues with what is written and remembered, and is present in the Preserved Tablet, every codex and every tongue. Nonetheless it remains numerically one despite the multiplication or destruction of codices. These are distinct accounts even within the broadly created-speech position.

Two familiar syllogisms are therefore set against one another. One yields the eternity of God's speech: it is an attribute of God, and His attributes are eternal. The other yields its origination: speech is a species of sound, and sounds originate. Both cannot be true in an unqualified sense of the same entity, so each party rejects a premise. Muʿtazilites deny that speech is an attribute subsisting in God; Karrāmiyya deny that every divine attribute is eternal; Ashʿarites deny that speech, properly so called, consists of sounds and letters; those designated ḥashwiyya deny that the articulated sequence must originate. Setting aside the author's criticisms of the latter two alternatives, the principal dispute between Ashʿarites and Muʿtazilites becomes the existence of internal speech and whether the Qurʾān names that internal speech or the ordered audible utterance. Both agree that the sensory utterance originates; if eternal internal speech were established, the Muʿtazila would not contest its eternity as an eternal divine attribute simply on that supposition. The report of Abū Ḥanīfa and Abū Yūsuf disputing for six months before judging the attribution “created” to the Qurʾān unbelief must, according to the author, be understood with this precise point of dispute in view.

First argument: a speaker is one in whom speech subsists

Our first proof is that the one properly called a speaker is the one in whom speech subsists, not merely someone who produces speech in another receptacle. The cause of movement in another body is not thereby called moving, nor is God called voiced simply because He creates sounds. Hearing someone utter “I am standing,” we call that person a speaker even if we do not know that he created the sound—and even if, following our doctrine, we know that God is the creator of the sound. Speech belonging to God must therefore subsist in Him; yet the sensory sequence of audible letters cannot subsist eternally in Him. It has a beginning and end, and one letter must be preceded by, and often conditioned on the ending of, the previous letter. Its parts do not exist simultaneously or endure after their utterance, as the earlier treatment of quantity explained. An originated accident cannot subsist in the divine essence. Hence the subsisting divine speech must be the meaning, since no third candidate for speech is available, and it must be eternal.

A Muʿtazilite objection holds that if speaking required a persisting accident in the subject, even human beings would not literally be called speakers: speech continually perishes and its sounds are located in the tongue rather than the whole person. Expressions such as “the prince speaks by the minister's tongue” and “the jinn speaks through the possessed person's tongue” also appear to separate speaker from substrate. A literalist objection says that the sequence of letters need not itself be successive: words are stored together in memory or impressed upon paper, and temporal order arises only when the bodily instrument of utterance produces them. The Qurʾān, encompassing order and meaning, could therefore be beginningless in God, even if the reading occurs in temporal order.

Reply: ordinary linguistic usage confirms that the speaker is the possessor of speech, and audible articulate sounds are necessarily successive and non-enduring. A transient accident may give a true name to its subject even without persisting, as with moving and speaking. Nor must an accident in every part of a bodily person inhere throughout the entire body for the person to be described by it; hearing, seeing and tasting operate through appropriate bodily parts. “Speaking through another's tongue” is figurative, signifying that the speaker supplies the words to another. The second objection changes the subject: the dispute concerns audible letters, not mental, remembered, depicted or written representations of them. Even an isolated, nonsuccessive sound is not a conceivable eternal attribute inhering in God's essence in the manner alleged.

Second argument: an internal discourse distinct from knowledge and volition

A person uttering a command, prohibition, call, assertion, question or other speech act finds something within the mind which is expressed in these forms. That which is mentally entertained does not vary simply because the outward expressions differ by the conventions of languages. The speaker intends it to occur in the hearer's understanding so that the hearer may act or respond accordingly. This is what we call speech of the soul or inward discourse. Abū Hāshim is said to acknowledge something like it under the designation thoughts (khawāṭir).

That this inward discourse differs from knowledge and will is especially evident in assertion and in expressive utterances that are not requests. One may mistakenly identify inward request with volition and regard “I want you to do this but do not request it inwardly,” or its converse, as contradictory. The discussion will return to this matter in the chapter on divine acts. For the moment, an assertion can concern what a person does not know, even what he knows to be false, which distinguishes the content of assertion from his knowledge. Likewise a master can command a slave to perform something without willing that it be performed, for instance to establish the slave's disobedience and furnish an excuse for punishment. This is offered as a distinction between command or request and volition.

Al-Mawāqif suggests that Muʿtazilites might explain these cases as a will to undertake an action which causes the hearer to believe that the speaker knows what he asserts, or wills what he commands. The present author observes that he has not found exactly this explanation in their texts, but he has found something resembling it in the Muʿtazilite al-Zāhidī, who calls these cases displays of the signs of asserting or requesting, rather than genuine informing and requesting. Imām al-Ḥaramayn also anticipates a similar reply in the Irshād: perhaps what one finds inwardly is only a will to cause an uttered expression to be a command of obligation or recommendation. The answer is that the utterance has already passed while the request remains; the bygone expression itself is not presently willed, but perhaps regretted or missed. The internal state continuing after the utterance is not merely regret. Furthermore the utterance clearly translates what is inwardly intended, namely requirement or imposition, not merely a wish to attach a specific grammatical force to the utterance.

Ordinary Arabic similarly applies “speech” or “saying” to what exists inwardly: “There is speech within me”; “I fashioned a saying in my mind.” The reported verse of al-Akhṭal locates speech in the heart and makes the tongue its indication, and revelation speaks of what people say within themselves. If God is genuinely a speaker, while sensory sounds cannot subsist in His essence, then speech subsisting in Him is this internal non-sensory reality and is eternal.

Objections concerning the Qurʾān and its revealed form

First and second Muʿtazilite objections: the Qurʾān is manifestly the ordered utterance of audible letters, a fact known in ordinary religious life even to the young, beginning with its praise of God and ending with the formula of seeking refuge; transmitted consensus identifies it in this way. Moreover its familiar properties known from text and consensus attach to the temporally originated arrangement, not to an internal eternal meaning. The response does not dispute that the name Qurʾān or speech of God is applied, through established linguistic usage or a well-known extension, to the sensory articulated form. This is the Quran commonly discussed by reciters, jurists and scholars of legal principles, and its letter-related properties are indeed originated.

The cited properties are these: the Qurʾān is remembrance (dhikr), and revelation describes newly arriving remembrance; it is Arabic, while the same meaning can be expressed in multiple languages, so being Arabic refers to its wording; it was sent down to the Prophet, while an eternal attribute subsisting in God's essence cannot literally move downward. An originated word, although an accident, can travel with the body or medium bearing it. The reports that the Qurʾān was first sent as a whole to the lower heaven, preserved or written there, and then conveyed gradually by Gabriel, are understood in this context. If someone argues that a manuscript contains only written shapes rather than sounds or concepts, one answers that writing signifies and represents words by the shapes of their letters. This distinction between represented word and the physical ink marks will matter below.

A third objection: the Qurʾān is the standing challenge (taḥaddī) to the Arabs to produce its equal. The challenge does not pertain to an eternal non-sensory attribute which remains perpetually beyond any specific occasion. Reply: the challenge is an event in which the Arabs are called to oppose the present articulated form by producing a comparable utterance; it is not a challenge to duplicate an eternal attribute. A fourth objection: the Qurʾān is subject to abrogation. Though a meaning as well as wording can be superseded, an eternal attribute cannot cease to exist; the kind of abrogation in question attaches to an originated wording or temporally applicable ruling.

A further proof from the divine 'Be!' is that the scriptural formula “Our word to something, when We will it, is only that We say to it 'Be!'” suggests a saying after willing to produce the thing and therefore an originated utterance. If one takes the word thing in the scope of the negation universally, however, an objection argues that even the saying “Be!” would need another preceding “Be!”, generating regress unless the saying is eternal. If the formula is merely figurative for immediate production, it loses force as evidence for an originated articulated speech. The reply examines the logic of the sentence: “Our saying to a thing when we bring it about is only this saying” restricts what is said when saying takes place; it does not entail that the saying is addressed to every thing, or that every saying is itself produced by a prior token of the same saying. Thus the asserted regress is not required by the wording.

In what sense do reciters and manuscripts bear God's speech?

A common account among our school identifies the articulated Qurʾān as God's speech simply because it indicates His eternal speech, so that the identity of the person inventing the letters would be irrelevant. The present author prefers to add another special connection to God: revelation describes God as the first producer of the recorded shapes in the Preserved Tablet, or of the sounds in the tongue of the angel, or of a verbal disclosure to the Prophet. The descent upon the Prophet's heart, in the cited verse, strictly concerns meaning rather than transported ink or sound.

Some therefore make the name Qurʾān denote the first individual ordered utterance whose existence God originated. Later individual readings acquired by human reciters are likenesses of that first utterance, not numerically it. The preferable account takes the name to denote the articulated form without specifying its first individual substrate; the Qurʾān is one by type, so that what each reader recites is the Qurʾān itself, not merely something called its likeness. The same difference arises for a poem or a book attributed to its author. On either account, the name can denote the complete text alone, or a common expression applying to the whole and to each portion; the question is treated further in the commentary on al-Tanqīḥ.

Accordingly, several statements receive different interpretations. “What is written in every codex and recited on every tongue is God's speech” concerns specific unity of form or type. “What is read is a narration or likeness of God's speech, and His speech proper is what was first produced in the angel's tongue” concerns individual identity. “God's speech is not in a tongue or heart and does not inhabit a codex or tablet” concerns the true eternal divine attribute. The use of “God's speech inhabits a codex or tongue” was discouraged even when referring to the originated wording, both out of reverence and because it easily misleads hearers into imagining that the eternal attribute itself inheres in the created substrate.

Another answer makes the predications “Arabic,” “revealed,” “recited,” “heard,” and “written” apply figuratively to the ancient meaning because they literally apply to the sounds and letters which indicate it. One similarly says “I heard that meaning from him,” “I read it in a book,” or “I wrote it with my hand,” while what was materially heard, read or written was its verbal and graphic representation. On this approach, recitation—the reader's acquired sounds—is originated, and writing—the writer's movement and the visible letter figures—is originated. What is recited, written, remembered in hearts, and heard can be called eternal insofar as it means what is understood through those sounds and markings, not an entity literally inhering in a tongue, heart, or codex. Likewise revelation can signify that Gabriel apprehends God's speech in his proper station, descends, and makes the Prophet understand what he had apprehended, without the eternal speech being displaced from God's essence.

Why is Moses singled out as the one spoken to by God?

If every believer may hear the originated Qurʾān and its eternal meaning can be understood through hearing, what marks Moses out as Kalīm Allāh? Several explanations are offered.

First, the view favored by al-Ghazālī, Moses heard the eternal speech without sound or letters, just as the divine essence may be seen in the Hereafter without bodily quantity or mode. This requires an account under which hearing, like vision, can be related to an existent other than sound, such an extraordinary relation being miraculous. Second, Moses heard a voice from all directions, contrary to ordinary hearing. Third, he heard it from a determinate direction, but in a sound that was not acquired by a created human agent: God Himself specially produced the voice and thus honored Moses with direct intelligible address. This last explanation is attributed to Abū Manṣūr al-Māturīdī and Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāyīnī. The latter reports that people agree that what is literally heard must be sound; some maintain that only sound is heard, while others apply heard to an inward meaning known through hearing sound, in which case the disagreement may be linguistic rather than substantive.

Objection: eternal speech would contain false past-tense reports

The truth of a past-tense assertion requires the reported relation to have already obtained. No event can be earlier than eternity. If these assertions were all literally eternal past-tense reports, they would have been false when eternity had not yet been succeeded by the relevant events, and divine falsehood is impossible.

Several grounds for denying divine falsehood are listed: scholarly consensus; the certain prophetic reports whose authenticity is established by miracles without depending on God's speaking; the judgment of reason that lying is a defect involving signs of ignorance, incapacity or vain activity; and the impossibility that a beginningless falsehood should subsequently become a truth, since what is beginningless cannot change into its contrary, although a knower of the relation can certainly state the relation as it actually holds. The created Qurʾānic wording is interpreted as an expression of the eternal speech so that truth and falsehood ultimately concern the signified content.

Yet there is a further doctrinal difficulty. Some Ashʿarites deny that one can argue divine truthfulness simply from lying's intrinsic badness, since they do not grant the Muʿtazilite doctrine of rational moral ugliness. Imām al-Ḥaramayn and the author of al-Talkhīṣ maintain that appealing to its badness either accepts an independently rational ethical value or makes an argument from revelation which presupposes the divine truthfulness it is meant to establish. The author of al-Mawāqif sees no clear difference between calling lying a defect in reason and judging it intrinsically ugly, and the present author voices surprise at these theologians' way of stating the issue. An argument from miracles as a special divine certification may, in his view, break the supposed circle; but this is not a question to suppress by terminology.

Those temporal descriptions arise later, through its relations to temporal things when their events and occasions obtain. The author nevertheless adds a striking qualification: explaining exactly how the eternal meaning is denoted by successive temporal wording is extremely difficult. So is an alternative that ascribes past, present and future entirely to the originated words while denying them to the eternal content. Both formulations require further thought.
